# OpenBMC Guide Tutorial

    

Welcome to the comprehensive OpenBMC development guide. This tutorial takes you from beginner to professional, covering everything from environment setup to advanced platform porting.

## What You’ll Learn

    

* **Getting Started**: Set up your development environment and build your first OpenBMC image
* **Architecture**: Understand OpenBMC’s D-Bus architecture, services, and design patterns
* **Core Services**: Master sensors, thermal management, power control, and system services
* **Interfaces**: Implement IPMI, Redfish, WebUI, and other management interfaces
* **Advanced Topics**: Debug features, security protocols (SPDM), and specialized components
* **Platform Porting**: Port OpenBMC to your custom hardware

## Quick Start

    

1. [Set up your environment](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/docs/01-getting-started/02-environment-setup.html)
2. [Build your first image](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/docs/01-getting-started/03-first-build.html)
3. [Understand the architecture](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/docs/02-architecture/01-openbmc-overview.html)

## Choose Your Path

    

Not sure where to start? We have [curated learning paths](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/learning-paths) for different experience levels and roles:

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Path | Best For |
| --- | --- |
| [Beginner](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/learning-paths#beginner-path) | New to OpenBMC, learning fundamentals |
| [Intermediate](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/learning-paths#intermediate-path) | Ready for core services and interfaces |
| [Advanced](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/learning-paths#advanced-path) | Complex topics and platform porting |
| [Software Developer](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/learning-paths#software-developer-path) | Writing OpenBMC services and code |
| [System Operator](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/learning-paths#system-operator-path) | Managing BMC-enabled servers |
| [Hardware Engineer](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/learning-paths#hardware-engineer-path) | Porting to new platforms |

</div>

## Prerequisites

    

* Linux development experience (command line, build systems)
* Basic C/C++ programming knowledge
* Familiarity with embedded systems concepts (helpful but not required)

## Sample Code

    

All examples in this guide are tested and available in the [examples/](https://github.com/MichaelTien8901/openbmc-guide-tutorial/tree/main/docs/examples) directory. Each example includes:

* Complete, buildable code
* README with setup instructions
* Verification steps for QEMU

Found an error? Want to add content? See our [Contributing Guide](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/contributing/).

## What is a BMC?

    

A **Baseboard Management Controller (BMC)** is a specialized microcontroller embedded on server motherboards. It provides **out-of-band management**, meaning it can monitor and control the server even when the main system is powered off or unresponsive.

### BMC Capabilities

    

* **Remote Power Control**: Power on/off, reset the server remotely
* **Hardware Monitoring**: Track temperatures, voltages, fan speeds
* **Console Access**: Serial-over-LAN for OS-independent access
* **Firmware Updates**: Update BIOS and other firmware remotely
* **Event Logging**: Record hardware events and errors
* **KVM**: Remote keyboard, video, mouse access
* **Virtual Media**: Mount remote images for OS installation

---

            direction TB

        subgraph BMC["BMC"]
            firmware["OpenBMC Firmware"]
        end
    end

    BMC -->|"Network: IPMI, Redfish, SSH"| DCIM["Data Center Management"]
```

│  │                        BMC                            │  │
│  │   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │  │
│  │   │              OpenBMC Firmware                │    │  │
│  │   └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                           │                                 │
│                           │ (Network: IPMI, Redfish, SSH)   │
│                           ▼                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                            │
                            ▼
                  ┌─────────────────┐
                  │ Data Center     │
                  │ Management      │
                  └─────────────────┘
```

</div>  </div>

---

## What is OpenBMC?

    

**OpenBMC** is a Linux distribution designed specifically for BMC firmware. It’s:

* **Open Source**: Apache 2.0 licensed, community-driven
* **Linux-Based**: Built on Yocto/Poky embedded Linux
* **Standards-Compliant**: Supports IPMI, Redfish, and modern protocols
* **Modular**: Component-based architecture via D-Bus

### Who Uses OpenBMC?

    

OpenBMC is used by major technology companies including:

* Facebook/Meta
* Google
* Microsoft
* IBM
* Intel
* Rackspace
* LinkedIn

### Why OpenBMC?

    

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Proprietary BMC | OpenBMC |
| --- | --- |
| Closed source, vendor lock-in | Open source, community-driven |
| Fixed feature set | Customizable to your needs |
| Security through obscurity | Auditable code, rapid patches |
| Vendor-specific interfaces | Standard interfaces (Redfish) |
| Limited extensibility | Fully extensible architecture |

</div>
---

## OpenBMC Architecture Overview

    

OpenBMC uses a modern, service-oriented architecture:

```mermaid
---
title: OpenBMC Architecture
---
flowchart TB
    subgraph interfaces["External Interfaces"]
        direction TB
        IPMI
        Redfish
        WebUI
        SSH
    end

    dbus["D-Bus (Inter-process Communication)"]

    subgraph services["Phosphor Services"]
        direction TB
        Sensors["Sensors Manager"]
        State["State Manager"]
        Logging["Logging Manager"]
    end

    subgraph kernel["Linux Kernel"]
        direction TB
        hwmon
        GPIO
        I2C
    end

    hardware["BMC Hardware (ASPEED AST2500/2600, Nuvoton)"]

    interfaces --> dbus
    dbus --> services
    services --> kernel
    kernel --> hardware
```

> **ASCII-art version (for comparison)**

  <div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    External Interfaces                      │
│   ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐    │
│   │   IPMI   │  │ Redfish  │  │  WebUI   │  │   SSH    │    │
│   └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                        D-Bus                                │
│            (Inter-process Communication)                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                    Phosphor Services                        │
│   ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐              │
│   │  Sensors   │ │   State    │ │  Logging   │  ...         │
│   │  Manager   │ │  Manager   │ │  Manager   │              │
│   └────────────┘ └────────────┘ └────────────┘              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                    Linux Kernel                             │
│   ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐              │
│   │   hwmon    │ │   GPIO     │ │    I2C     │  ...         │
│   └────────────┘ └────────────┘ └────────────┘              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                    BMC Hardware                             │
│              (ASPEED AST2500/2600, Nuvoton)                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

</div>  </div>

### Key Components

    

* **D-Bus**: Central communication bus connecting all services
* **Phosphor Services**: Modular daemons for specific functions
* **bmcweb**: HTTP server for Redfish and WebUI
* **ipmid**: IPMI command processing
* **systemd**: Service management

## Development Environment

    

### QEMU: The Standard Development Platform

    

OpenBMC development does **not require physical BMC hardware**. QEMU emulation is the standard development environment used by professional OpenBMC developers at major companies.

```mermaid
---
title: QEMU Development Environment
---
flowchart LR
    subgraph DevMachine["Your Development Machine"]
        subgraph QEMU["QEMU (ast2600-evb)"]
            subgraph image["OpenBMC Image"]
            features["D-Bus services, Redfish API,  
IPMI daemon, Sensors,  
State management"]
            end
        end

        QEMU -->|"Port forwarding:  
SSH, HTTPS, IPMI"| testing

        testing["Test with: curl, ipmitool, ssh, browser"]
    end
```

> **ASCII-art version (for comparison)**

  <div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  Your Development Machine                    │
│                                                             │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │                   QEMU (ast2600-evb)                │   │
│   │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │   │
│   │  │              OpenBMC Image                    │  │   │
│   │  │                                               │  │   │
│   │  │  • Full D-Bus services                       │  │   │
│   │  │  • Redfish API (bmcweb)                      │  │   │
│   │  │  • IPMI daemon                               │  │   │
│   │  │  • Sensor management                         │  │   │
│   │  │  • State management                          │  │   │
│   │  │  • All phosphor-* services                   │  │   │
│   │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │   │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                            │                                 │
│              Port forwarding: SSH, HTTPS, IPMI              │
│                            ▼                                 │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │  Test with: curl, ipmitool, ssh, browser           │   │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

</div>  </div>

### What You Can Learn with QEMU

    

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Topic | QEMU Support | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenBMC architecture | ✅ Full | All services run identically |
| D-Bus communication | ✅ Full | Same as real hardware |
| Redfish API development | ✅ Full | Complete API available |
| IPMI commands | ✅ Full | ipmitool works |
| Yocto/BitBake builds | ✅ Full | Standard workflow |
| Service development | ✅ Full | Code, build, test cycle |
| Sensor configuration | ✅ Simulated | Values are synthetic |
| Fan control logic | ✅ Simulated | PID algorithms work |

</div>

Physical BMC hardware (ASPEED AST2600 EVB ~$500+) is only needed for hardware bring-up tasks like eSPI debugging, PECI communication, or real sensor calibration. These are specialized topics not required for learning OpenBMC software development.

## Overview

    

This guide covers three setup options:

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Option | Best For | Host OS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Native Linux** | Full performance, serious development | Ubuntu/Fedora |
| **Docker** | Quick start, Windows/macOS users | Any |
| **SDK Only** | Application development without full builds | Any |

</div>

Choose the option that fits your needs. For complete OpenBMC development, **Native Linux** is recommended.

---

## System Requirements

    

### Minimum Requirements

    

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Resource | Minimum | Recommended |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **OS** | Ubuntu 20.04, Fedora 34 | Ubuntu 22.04, Fedora 38 |
| **RAM** | 16 GB | 32 GB |
| **Disk** | 100 GB free | 250 GB SSD |
| **CPU** | 4 cores | 8+ cores |

</div>

Building OpenBMC is resource-intensive. Insufficient RAM will cause build failures.

---

## Option 1: Native Linux Setup (Recommended)

    

### Ubuntu 22.04 / 20.04

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Update system</span>
<span class="nb">sudo </span>apt update <span class="o">&&</span> <span class="nb">sudo </span>apt upgrade <span class="nt">-y</span>

<span class="c"># Install required packages</span>
<span class="nb">sudo </span>apt <span class="nb">install</span> <span class="nt">-y</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    gawk wget git diffstat unzip texinfo gcc build-essential <span class="se">\</span>
    chrpath socat cpio python3 python3-pip python3-pexpect <span class="se">\</span>
    xz-utils debianutils iputils-ping python3-git python3-jinja2 <span class="se">\</span>
    libegl1-mesa libsdl1.2-dev pylint xterm python3-subunit <span class="se">\</span>
    mesa-common-dev zstd liblz4-tool

<span class="c"># Install additional useful tools</span>
<span class="nb">sudo </span>apt <span class="nb">install</span> <span class="nt">-y</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    curl vim tmux htop tree <span class="se">\</span>
    libssl-dev libffi-dev

<span class="c"># Verify installation</span>
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"Checking installed tools..."</span>
git <span class="nt">--version</span>
python3 <span class="nt">--version</span>
gcc <span class="nt">--version</span>
```

</div></div>

### Fedora 38 / 34

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Install required packages</span>
<span class="nb">sudo </span>dnf <span class="nb">install</span> <span class="nt">-y</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    gawk make wget <span class="nb">tar </span>bzip2 <span class="nb">gzip </span>python3 unzip perl patch <span class="se">\</span>
    diffutils diffstat git cpp gcc gcc-c++ glibc-devel <span class="se">\</span>
    texinfo chrpath ccache perl-Data-Dumper perl-Text-ParseWords <span class="se">\</span>
    perl-Thread-Queue perl-bignum socat python3-pexpect <span class="se">\</span>
    findutils which file cpio python python3-pip xz python3-GitPython <span class="se">\</span>
    python3-jinja2 SDL-devel xterm rpcgen mesa-libGL-devel <span class="se">\</span>
    perl-FindBin perl-File-Compare perl-File-Copy perl-locale <span class="se">\</span>
    zstd lz4

<span class="c"># Verify installation</span>
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"Checking installed tools..."</span>
git <span class="nt">--version</span>
python3 <span class="nt">--version</span>
gcc <span class="nt">--version</span>
```

</div></div>

### Clone OpenBMC Repository

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Create workspace directory</span>
<span class="nb">mkdir</span> <span class="nt">-p</span> ~/openbmc-workspace
<span class="nb">cd</span> ~/openbmc-workspace

<span class="c"># Clone the repository</span>
git clone https://github.com/openbmc/openbmc.git
<span class="nb">cd </span>openbmc

<span class="c"># Check available machines</span>
<span class="nb">ls </span>meta-<span class="k">*</span>/meta-<span class="k">*</span>/conf/machine/<span class="k">*</span>.conf | <span class="nb">head</span> <span class="nt">-20</span>
```

</div></div>

### Initialize Build Environment

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Source the environment script</span>
<span class="c"># This sets up paths and creates the build directory</span>
<span class="nb">.</span> setup ast2600-evb

<span class="c"># You're now in the build directory</span>
<span class="c"># The terminal prompt changes to indicate the environment is active</span>
```

</div></div>

`ast2600-evb` is an AST2600-based evaluation board, ideal for learning modern OpenBMC. Replace with your target machine for production development.

## Option 2: Docker Setup

    

Docker provides a consistent build environment across operating systems.

### Install Docker

    

**Ubuntu/Debian:**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Install Docker</span>
curl <span class="nt">-fsSL</span> https://get.docker.com <span class="nt">-o</span> get-docker.sh
<span class="nb">sudo </span>sh get-docker.sh

<span class="c"># Add user to docker group (logout/login required)</span>
<span class="nb">sudo </span>usermod <span class="nt">-aG</span> docker <span class="nv">$USER</span>
```

</div></div>

**Windows/macOS:**
Download and install [Docker Desktop](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/).

### Using the OpenBMC Build Container

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Create workspace</span>
<span class="nb">mkdir</span> <span class="nt">-p</span> ~/openbmc-workspace
<span class="nb">cd</span> ~/openbmc-workspace

<span class="c"># Clone OpenBMC</span>
git clone https://github.com/openbmc/openbmc.git
<span class="nb">cd </span>openbmc

<span class="c"># Run build in container</span>
docker run <span class="nt">--rm</span> <span class="nt">-it</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-v</span> <span class="si">$(</span><span class="nb">pwd</span><span class="si">)</span>:/home/openbmc/openbmc <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-w</span> /home/openbmc/openbmc <span class="se">\</span>
    crops/poky:ubuntu-22.04 <span class="se">\</span>
    /bin/bash <span class="nt">-c</span> <span class="s2">". setup ast2600-evb && bitbake obmc-phosphor-image"</span>
```

</div></div>

### Custom Dockerfile (Alternative)

    

Create a `Dockerfile` for a customized environment:

<div class="language-dockerfile highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="k">FROM</span><span class="s"> ubuntu:22.04</span>

<span class="k">ENV</span><span class="s"> DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive</span>

<span class="k">RUN </span>apt-get update <span class="o">&&</span> apt-get <span class="nb">install</span> <span class="nt">-y</span> <span class="se">\
</span>    gawk wget git diffstat unzip texinfo gcc build-essential <span class="se">\
</span>    chrpath socat cpio python3 python3-pip python3-pexpect <span class="se">\
</span>    xz-utils debianutils iputils-ping python3-git python3-jinja2 <span class="se">\
</span>    libegl1-mesa libsdl1.2-dev pylint xterm python3-subunit <span class="se">\
</span>    mesa-common-dev zstd liblz4-tool locales <span class="se">\
</span>    <span class="o">&&</span> <span class="nb">rm</span> <span class="nt">-rf</span> /var/lib/apt/lists/<span class="k">*</span>

<span class="c"># Set locale</span>
<span class="k">RUN </span>locale-gen en_US.UTF-8
<span class="k">ENV</span><span class="s"> LANG=en_US.UTF-8</span>

<span class="c"># Create non-root user</span>
<span class="k">RUN </span>useradd <span class="nt">-ms</span> /bin/bash openbmc
<span class="k">USER</span><span class="s"> openbmc</span>
<span class="k">WORKDIR</span><span class="s"> /home/openbmc</span>

<span class="k">CMD</span><span class="s"> ["/bin/bash"]</span>
```

</div></div>

Build and use:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
docker build <span class="nt">-t</span> openbmc-builder <span class="nb">.</span>
docker run <span class="nt">--rm</span> <span class="nt">-it</span> <span class="nt">-v</span> <span class="si">$(</span><span class="nb">pwd</span><span class="si">)</span>:/home/openbmc/openbmc openbmc-builder
```

</div></div>

## Option 3: SDK Installation

    

The SDK allows cross-compiling applications without a full build environment.

### Generate SDK (requires full build first)

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># In an initialized build environment</span>
bitbake obmc-phosphor-image <span class="nt">-c</span> populate_sdk
```

</div></div>

The SDK installer is created at:

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
build/tmp/deploy/sdk/oecore-x86_64-arm1176jzs-toolchain-*.sh
```

</div></div>

### Install SDK

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Run the installer</span>
./oecore-x86_64-arm1176jzs-toolchain-<span class="k">*</span>.sh

<span class="c"># Default install location: /opt/openbmc-phosphor/VERSION</span>
<span class="c"># Accept the default or specify a custom path</span>
```

</div></div>

### Use SDK

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Source the environment</span>
<span class="nb">source</span> /opt/openbmc-phosphor/VERSION/environment-setup-arm1176jzs-openbmc-linux-gnueabi

<span class="c"># Verify cross-compiler</span>
<span class="nv">$CC</span> <span class="nt">--version</span>
<span class="c"># Should show arm-openbmc-linux-gnueabi-gcc</span>

<span class="c"># Cross-compile a simple program</span>
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s1">'int main() { return 0; }'</span> <span class="o">></span> test.c
<span class="nv">$CC</span> test.c <span class="nt">-o</span> <span class="nb">test
</span>file <span class="nb">test</span>
<span class="c"># Should show: ELF 32-bit LSB executable, ARM</span>
```

</div></div>
---

## QEMU Setup

    

QEMU allows testing OpenBMC without physical hardware.

### Install QEMU

    

**Ubuntu 24.04+ / Fedora 38+:**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Ubuntu</span>
<span class="nb">sudo </span>apt <span class="nb">install</span> <span class="nt">-y</span> qemu-system-arm

<span class="c"># Fedora</span>
<span class="nb">sudo </span>dnf <span class="nb">install</span> <span class="nt">-y</span> qemu-system-arm
```

</div></div>

### Verify QEMU Has ASPEED Support

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Check version (need 7.0+ for ast2600-evb)</span>
qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">--version</span>

<span class="c"># Verify ast2600-evb machine is available</span>
qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">-machine</span> <span class="nb">help</span> | <span class="nb">grep </span>ast2600
```

</div></div>

**Older distributions** (Ubuntu 20.04/22.04, Debian 11) may not have ast2600-evb support in their package QEMU. If `grep ast2600` returns nothing, see [Building QEMU](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/docs/01-getting-started/05-qemu-build.html) to build from source or use OpenBMC’s built-in QEMU.

QEMU usage is covered in the [First Build](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/docs/01-getting-started/03-first-build.html) guide.

## IDE Setup (VS Code)

    

VS Code provides excellent support for OpenBMC development.

### Install VS Code

    

Download from [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/)

### Recommended Extensions

    

Install these extensions:

* **C/C++** (Microsoft) - IntelliSense, debugging
* **Remote - SSH** - Remote development
* **Remote - Containers** - Docker development
* **Python** - Python support
* **YAML** - Recipe file editing
* **BitBake** - Yocto syntax highlighting

### Configure IntelliSense

    

Create `.vscode/c_cpp_properties.json`:

<div class="language-json highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"configurations"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"name"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"OpenBMC"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"includePath"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[</span><span class="w">
                </span><span class="s2">"${workspaceFolder}/**"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
                </span><span class="s2">"/path/to/sdk/sysroots/arm*/usr/include/**"</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="p">],</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"defines"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[],</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"compilerPath"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"/path/to/sdk/sysroots/x86_64*/usr/bin/arm-openbmc-linux-gnueabi-gcc"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"cStandard"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"c17"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"cppStandard"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"c++20"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"intelliSenseMode"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"linux-gcc-arm"</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="p">],</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"version"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">4</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
</span>
```

</div></div>

### VS Code Dev Container (Recommended for Docker Users)

    

A ready-to-use Dev Container configuration provides a complete OpenBMC build environment with pre-configured tools, extensions, and build caching. The devcontainer is designed to live inside the openbmc repo itself — you open the openbmc repo in VS Code and everything works.

#### Prerequisites

    

* [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) with the [Dev Containers](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-vscode-remote.remote-containers) extension
* [Docker Desktop](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/) (Windows/macOS) or Docker Engine (Linux)

#### Setup Steps

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># 1. Clone OpenBMC</span>
git clone https://github.com/openbmc/openbmc.git
<span class="nb">cd </span>openbmc

<span class="c"># 2. Add the devcontainer configuration (download from this tutorial site)</span>
<span class="nb">mkdir</span> <span class="nt">-p</span> .devcontainer
<span class="nv">base</span><span class="o">=</span>https://michaeltien8901.github.io/openbmc-guide-tutorial/docs/examples/devcontainer
curl <span class="nt">-fsSL</span> <span class="nt">-o</span> .devcontainer/devcontainer.json <span class="s2">"</span><span class="nv">$base</span><span class="s2">/devcontainer.json"</span>
curl <span class="nt">-fsSL</span> <span class="nt">-o</span> .devcontainer/Dockerfile        <span class="s2">"</span><span class="nv">$base</span><span class="s2">/Dockerfile"</span>

<span class="c"># 3. Open in VS Code</span>
code <span class="nb">.</span>
```

</div></div>

Then in VS Code, press **F1** → **Dev Containers: Reopen in Container**. The first build takes several minutes; subsequent opens use cached layers.

The [`docs/examples/devcontainer/`](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/docs/examples/devcontainer/devcontainer.json) directory in this tutorial holds the reference `Dockerfile` and `devcontainer.json`. The commands above download them into your openbmc clone as `.devcontainer/`; you can also browse them in the [tutorial repo](https://github.com/MichaelTien8901/openbmc-guide-tutorial/tree/main/docs/examples/devcontainer).

#### What You Get

    

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| **Base image** | Ubuntu 24.04 with all Yocto/BitBake dependencies |
| **User** | `openbmc` with `sudo` access; UID auto-mapped to your host UID |
| **Build caching** | `sstate-cache` and `downloads` persist in Docker volumes across rebuilds |
| **Build env** | `oe-init-build-env` sourced automatically; `PARALLEL_MAKE` and `BB_NUMBER_THREADS` set to `$(nproc)` |
| **QEMU** | `qemu-system-arm` 8.2+ pre-installed with ast2600-evb support |
| **Extensions** | C/C++, Python, YAML, BitBake, GitLens, Git Graph, Code Spell Checker |
| **Forwarded ports** | 2222 (BMC SSH), 2443 (BMC HTTPS/Redfish), 2623 (BMC IPMI) |

</div>

#### Building OpenBMC Inside the Container

    

Once the container starts, the terminal is inside the openbmc repo with the build environment initialized:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Build the full image</span>
bitbake obmc-phosphor-image

<span class="c"># Or build a single recipe</span>
bitbake phosphor-webui
```

</div></div>

#### Build Caching with Docker Volumes

    

BitBake uses two large directories during builds:

* **`downloads/`** (`DL_DIR`) — upstream source tarballs fetched from the internet (several GB)
* **`sstate-cache/`** (`SSTATE_DIR`) — shared state cache of previously compiled outputs (saves hours on rebuilds)

The Dev Container mounts both as **Docker named volumes** rather than bind mounts:

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
source=openbmc-downloads,target=<workspace>/build/downloads,type=volume
source=openbmc-sstate-cache,target=<workspace>/build/sstate-cache,type=volume
```

</div></div>

This means:

* The data lives on your host in Docker-managed storage (`/var/lib/docker/volumes/`), **not** inside the container
* Deleting or rebuilding the container does not lose cached data
* **No `local.conf` configuration needed** — BitBake’s default `DL_DIR` (`build/downloads/`) matches the mount target, so it works automatically
* **Shared across projects** — any container using the same volume name (e.g., `openbmc-downloads`) shares the same downloaded sources, avoiding redundant multi-GB downloads

`docker system prune` does **not** delete named volumes. To fully reset build caches, explicitly remove them: `docker volume rm openbmc-sstate-cache openbmc-downloads`.

#### Using Dev Container from the CLI (Without VS Code)

    

You can use the Dev Container from any terminal using the [Dev Container CLI](https://github.com/devcontainers/cli):

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Install the CLI</span>
npm <span class="nb">install</span> <span class="nt">-g</span> @devcontainers/cli

<span class="c"># Build and start the container (from your openbmc clone with .devcontainer/)</span>
devcontainer up <span class="nt">--workspace-folder</span> ./openbmc

<span class="c"># Open an interactive shell inside it</span>
devcontainer <span class="nb">exec</span> <span class="nt">--workspace-folder</span> ./openbmc bash

<span class="c"># Run a single command</span>
devcontainer <span class="nb">exec</span> <span class="nt">--workspace-folder</span> ./openbmc <span class="se">\</span>
    bitbake obmc-phosphor-image
```

</div></div>

#### Git Identity

    

The container does **not** set a git identity — it inherits your host’s git configuration. If git prompts you to set `user.name` and `user.email`, configure them either on your host or inside the container:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
git config <span class="nt">--global</span> user.name <span class="s2">"Your Name"</span>
git config <span class="nt">--global</span> user.email <span class="s2">"you@example.com"</span>
```

</div></div>

#### Troubleshooting Dev Container

    

**File permission issues:**
The `updateRemoteUserUID` setting should handle this automatically. If you still see permission errors, rebuild the container: **F1** → **Dev Containers: Rebuild Container**.

---

## Best Practices: Container-Based Environment

    

Whether you are a solo developer or part of a team, a container-based workflow provides reproducibility and faster onboarding. This section covers recommended setups for both scenarios.

### Individual Developer Setup

    

For a single developer, the goal is a reproducible environment with persistent build caches.

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
Host Machine
├── openbmc/                     # Git clone (bind mount into container)
│   └── .devcontainer/           # Dev Container config
└── Docker Volumes
    ├── openbmc-sstate-cache     # Persists across container rebuilds
    └── openbmc-downloads        # Shared source tarballs
```

</div></div>

**Key practices:**

1. **Use named Docker volumes for build caches** — not bind mounts. Named volumes have better I/O performance and survive container rebuilds.
2. **Pin your container image** — use a specific tag (e.g., `ubuntu:24.04`), not `latest`. This prevents surprise breakages when the base image updates.
3. **Keep source on host, tools in container** — bind-mount your openbmc clone so you edit with your host IDE. All build tooling lives in the container.
4. **Pre-build the SDK once, reuse it** — generate the SDK inside the container and install it to a named volume:

    
```
# Inside container: build SDK
bitbake obmc-phosphor-image -c populate_sdk

# Install to a persistent volume
./tmp/deploy/sdk/oecore-*.sh -d /opt/openbmc-sdk -y
```

    

    Mount `/opt/openbmc-sdk` as a named volume so you can use it without rebuilding.
5. **Use ccache for kernel/u-boot iteration** — add to your `local.conf`:

    
```
INHERIT += "ccache"
CCACHE_TOP_DIR = "${TOPDIR}/ccache"
```

    

    Mount `ccache/` as a named volume for persistence.

### Team / Project Setup

    

For teams, the goal is shared caches, consistent environments, and fast onboarding for new members.

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
┌───────────────────────────┐
                 │     CI Server             │
                 │  (nightly full build)     │
                 │                           │
                 │  ┌─ sstate-cache ───────┐ │
                 │  │  (published via HTTP)│ │
                 │  └──────────────────────┘ │
                 │  ┌─ SDK installer ──────┐ │
                 │  │  (published to       │ │
                 │  │   registry/storage)  │ │
                 │  └──────────────────────┘ │
                 │  ┌─ Container image ────┐ │
                 │  │  (pushed to registry)│ │
                 │  └──────────────────────┘ │
                 └────────────┬──────────────┘
                              │
              ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
              ▼               ▼               ▼
         Developer A     Developer B     Developer C
         (pulls image,   (same image,    (new hire,
          uses sstate     uses sstate     onboards in
          mirror)         mirror)         minutes)
```

</div></div>

#### 1. Publish a team container image

    

Build a single container image in CI and push it to your registry:

<div class="language-dockerfile highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="k">FROM</span><span class="s"> ubuntu:24.04</span>

<span class="k">ENV</span><span class="s"> DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive</span>

<span class="k">RUN </span>apt-get update <span class="o">&&</span> apt-get <span class="nb">install</span> <span class="nt">-y</span> <span class="se">\
</span>    gawk wget git diffstat unzip texinfo gcc build-essential <span class="se">\
</span>    chrpath socat cpio python3 python3-pip python3-pexpect <span class="se">\
</span>    xz-utils debianutils iputils-ping python3-git python3-jinja2 <span class="se">\
</span>    libegl1-mesa libsdl1.2-dev pylint python3-subunit <span class="se">\
</span>    mesa-common-dev zstd liblz4-tool locales <span class="se">\
</span>    qemu-system-arm ccache <span class="se">\
</span>    <span class="o">&&</span> <span class="nb">rm</span> <span class="nt">-rf</span> /var/lib/apt/lists/<span class="k">*</span>

<span class="k">RUN </span>locale-gen en_US.UTF-8
<span class="k">ENV</span><span class="s"> LANG=en_US.UTF-8</span>

<span class="k">RUN </span>useradd <span class="nt">-ms</span> /bin/bash openbmc
<span class="k">USER</span><span class="s"> openbmc</span>
<span class="k">WORKDIR</span><span class="s"> /home/openbmc</span>
```

</div></div>

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># CI builds and pushes</span>
docker build <span class="nt">-t</span> registry.company.com/openbmc-builder:2024.04 <span class="nb">.</span>
docker push registry.company.com/openbmc-builder:2024.04
```

</div></div>

Tag images by date or build number, not `latest`. This lets developers pin to a known-good version while allowing controlled upgrades.

#### 2. Share sstate cache via HTTP

    

This is the single biggest time saver for teams. CI builds the full image nightly and publishes sstate:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># On CI: after full build completes, sync sstate to web server</span>
rsync <span class="nt">-a</span> build/sstate-cache/ /var/www/sstate/

<span class="c"># On developer machines: add to build/conf/local.conf</span>
SSTATE_MIRRORS <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s2">"file://.* http://build-server.company.com/sstate/PATH"</span>
```

</div></div>

With a shared sstate mirror, a developer’s first build downloads pre-compiled artifacts instead of compiling from scratch — reducing build time from hours to minutes.

#### 3. Distribute a pre-built SDK

    

For developers who only work on applications (daemons, D-Bus services) and do not need full image builds:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># CI: build and publish SDK</span>
bitbake obmc-phosphor-image <span class="nt">-c</span> populate_sdk
<span class="c"># Upload installer to artifact storage (e.g., Artifactory, S3, NFS)</span>

<span class="c"># Developer: download and install</span>
./oecore-x86_64-arm1176jzs-toolchain-<span class="k">*</span>.sh <span class="nt">-d</span> /opt/openbmc-sdk <span class="nt">-y</span>
<span class="nb">source</span> /opt/openbmc-sdk/environment-setup-<span class="k">*</span>
<span class="c"># Now compile directly — no BitBake needed</span>
<span class="nv">$CC</span> <span class="nt">-o</span> my_daemon my_daemon.c <span class="si">$(</span>pkg-config <span class="nt">--cflags</span> <span class="nt">--libs</span> sdbusplus<span class="si">)</span>
```

</div></div>

Or ship the SDK inside a container image:

<div class="language-dockerfile highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="k">FROM</span><span class="s"> ubuntu:24.04</span>
<span class="k">COPY</span><span class="s"> openbmc-sdk-installer.sh /tmp/</span>
<span class="k">RUN </span>/tmp/openbmc-sdk-installer.sh <span class="nt">-d</span> /opt/openbmc-sdk <span class="nt">-y</span> <span class="o">&&</span> <span class="nb">rm</span> /tmp/<span class="k">*</span>.sh
<span class="k">ENV</span><span class="s"> PATH="/opt/openbmc-sdk/sysroots/x86_64-oesdk-linux/usr/bin:$PATH"</span>
<span class="k">ENTRYPOINT</span><span class="s"> ["/bin/bash", "-c", "source /opt/openbmc-sdk/environment-setup-* && exec bash"]</span>
```

</div></div>

New developers `docker pull` and start coding immediately.

#### 4. Docker Compose for the full stack

    

For teams that need both the build environment and sstate mirror running locally:

<div class="language-yaml highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c1"># docker-compose.yml</span>
<span class="na">services</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">builder</span><span class="pi">:</span>
    <span class="na">image</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">registry.company.com/openbmc-builder:2024.04</span>
    <span class="na">volumes</span><span class="pi">:</span>
      <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s">./openbmc:/home/openbmc/openbmc</span>
      <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s">sstate-cache:/home/openbmc/openbmc/build/sstate-cache</span>
      <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s">downloads:/home/openbmc/openbmc/build/downloads</span>
    <span class="na">stdin_open</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="kc">true</span>
    <span class="na">tty</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="kc">true</span>

  <span class="na">sstate-mirror</span><span class="pi">:</span>
    <span class="na">image</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">nginx:alpine</span>
    <span class="na">volumes</span><span class="pi">:</span>
      <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s">sstate-cache:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro</span>
    <span class="na">ports</span><span class="pi">:</span>
      <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="s">8080:80"</span>

<span class="na">volumes</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">sstate-cache</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">downloads</span><span class="pi">:</span>
```

</div></div>

This gives each developer a local sstate mirror that other containers or native builds can reference.

### Summary: Which Setup to Use

    

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Scenario | Recommended Approach |
| --- | --- |
| Solo developer, full builds | Dev Container + named volumes for sstate/downloads |
| Solo developer, app only | Pre-built SDK (native or in container) |
| Team, full builds | Team container image + shared sstate HTTP mirror |
| Team, app developers | Pre-built SDK container from CI |
| Team, CI/CD | Nightly full build → publish sstate + SDK + container image |

</div>

The common theme across all setups: **build expensive artifacts once, share them everywhere**. Whether it is sstate, SDK, or container images, avoid having each developer rebuild what has already been built.

## Troubleshooting

    

### Build fails with “out of memory”

    

Increase system RAM or add swap:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="nb">sudo </span>fallocate <span class="nt">-l</span> 8G /swapfile
<span class="nb">sudo chmod </span>600 /swapfile
<span class="nb">sudo </span>mkswap /swapfile
<span class="nb">sudo </span>swapon /swapfile
```

</div></div>

### Permission denied with Docker

    

Ensure user is in the docker group:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="nb">sudo </span>usermod <span class="nt">-aG</span> docker <span class="nv">$USER</span>
<span class="c"># Then logout and login</span>
```

</div></div>

### “locale” errors during build

    

Set locale:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="nb">export </span><span class="nv">LANG</span><span class="o">=</span>en_US.UTF-8
<span class="nb">export </span><span class="nv">LC_ALL</span><span class="o">=</span>en_US.UTF-8
```

</div></div>

## Overview

    

This guide walks you through building an OpenBMC image and running it in QEMU.

**QEMU is not a compromise** — it’s the standard development environment used by professional OpenBMC developers. You’ll have access to 100% of the OpenBMC software stack, including all D-Bus services, Redfish API, IPMI, and management interfaces.

---

## Clone OpenBMC

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Clone the OpenBMC repository</span>
git clone https://github.com/openbmc/openbmc.git
<span class="nb">cd </span>openbmc
```

</div></div>
---

## Initialize Build Environment

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Set up environment for ast2600-evb machine (QEMU-compatible)</span>
<span class="nb">.</span> setup ast2600-evb

<span class="c"># This creates a build directory and configures for ast2600-evb</span>
```

</div></div>
---

## Build the Image

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Build the full image (this takes 1-4 hours first time)</span>
bitbake obmc-phosphor-image

<span class="c"># For faster iteration, build minimal image</span>
bitbake obmc-phosphor-image-minimal
```

</div></div>

### Build Tips

    

* First build downloads many sources - be patient
* Subsequent builds are much faster (incremental)
* Use `bitbake -c cleansstate ` to rebuild a package

---

## Run in QEMU

    

QEMU provides a complete OpenBMC environment where you can:

* Access all D-Bus services exactly as on real hardware
* Test Redfish API endpoints with curl or any HTTP client
* Use ipmitool for IPMI commands
* SSH into the BMC and run commands
* Develop and debug services with full functionality

### Locate the Image

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Find the built image</span>
<span class="nb">ls </span>tmp/deploy/images/ast2600-evb/

<span class="c"># Key files:</span>
<span class="c"># - obmc-phosphor-image-ast2600-evb.static.mtd (flash image)</span>
<span class="c"># - fitImage-obmc-phosphor-initramfs-ast2600-evb (kernel)</span>
```

</div></div>

### Start QEMU

    

**QEMU 7.0+ is required** for ast2600-evb support. Stock QEMU on Ubuntu 20.04/22.04 may not include this machine. Check with `qemu-system-arm -machine help | grep ast2600`. If not found, see [Building QEMU](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/docs/01-getting-started/05-qemu-build.html).

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Run QEMU manually:</span>
qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">-m</span> 1G <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-M</span> ast2600-evb <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-nographic</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-drive</span> <span class="nv">file</span><span class="o">=</span>tmp/deploy/images/ast2600-evb/obmc-phosphor-image-ast2600-evb.static.mtd,format<span class="o">=</span>raw,if<span class="o">=</span>mtd <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-net</span> nic <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-net</span> user,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>tcp::2222-:22,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>tcp::2443-:443,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>udp::2623-:623
```

</div></div>

### Default Credentials

    

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Interface | Username | Password |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SSH | root | 0penBmc |
| Redfish | root | 0penBmc |
| WebUI | root | 0penBmc |

</div>
---

### Build Fails

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Check for missing dependencies</span>

```

# Development Workflow

    

Iterate quickly on OpenBMC code using devtool, recipe customization, and build optimization.

</li>
  <li><a href="#recipe-customization-with-bbappend" id="markdown-toc-recipe-customization-with-bbappend">Recipe Customization with bbappend</a>    
1. [bbappend Naming Conventions](#bbappend-naming-conventions)
2. [bbappend Directory Structure](#bbappend-directory-structure)
3. [Common bbappend Use Cases](#common-bbappend-use-cases)
4. [Layer Priority](#layer-priority)
5. [When to Upstream vs Maintain Local Patches](#when-to-upstream-vs-maintain-local-patches)

  </li>
  <li><a href="#build-optimization" id="markdown-toc-build-optimization">Build Optimization</a>    
1. [Enable ccache](#enable-ccache)
2. [Configure sstate Cache](#configure-sstate-cache)
3. [Parallel Build Configuration](#parallel-build-configuration)
4. [Verify Optimization is Working](#verify-optimization-is-working)

  </li>
  <li><a href="#troubleshooting" id="markdown-toc-troubleshooting">Troubleshooting</a>    
1. [devtool Workspace Conflicts](#devtool-workspace-conflicts)
2. [sstate Cache Misses](#sstate-cache-misses)
3. [Workspace Inspection Commands](#workspace-inspection-commands)

  </li>
  <li><a href="#next-steps" id="markdown-toc-next-steps">Next Steps</a></li>
</ol>

**Yocto Compatibility**: This guide is tested with OpenBMC on Yocto Kirkstone and Scarthgap releases. Command syntax may vary slightly on older releases.

## Overview

    

After completing your first build, you’ll want to modify OpenBMC code and test changes quickly. A full `bitbake` rebuild can take 30+ minutes, but with the right workflow you can iterate in under 5 minutes.

This guide covers three essential techniques:

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Technique | Use Case | Time Savings |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **devtool** | Modify and test a single recipe | 30 min → 2 min |
| **bbappend** | Sustainable recipe customization | Avoid upstream conflicts |
| **Build optimization** | Faster overall builds | 2-4x speedup |

</div>
---

## devtool Workflow

    

`devtool` is your primary tool for rapid iteration. It extracts recipe source code to a workspace where you can edit, build, and test without full rebuilds.

### When to Use devtool vs bitbake

    

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Scenario | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Modifying existing recipe source code | `devtool` |
| Adding debug output to a service | `devtool` |
| Building entire image from scratch | `bitbake` |
| Creating permanent recipe customization | `bbappend` |

</div>

### devtool modify - Extract Source Code

    

Extract a recipe’s source code to your workspace for editing:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Initialize build environment first</span>
<span class="nb">cd </span>openbmc
<span class="nb">.</span> setup ast2600-evb

<span class="c"># Extract phosphor-logging source to workspace</span>
devtool modify phosphor-logging

<span class="c"># Source is now at:</span>
<span class="c"># workspace/sources/phosphor-logging/</span>
```

</div></div>

The workspace directory structure:

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
workspace/
├── sources/
│   └── phosphor-logging/    # Editable source code
└── appends/
    └── phosphor-logging.bbappend  # Auto-generated append
```

</div></div>

The `devtool modify` command automatically creates a bbappend that redirects the build to use your workspace source instead of fetching from upstream.

### devtool build - Incremental Build

    

After modifying source code, rebuild just that recipe:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Build only phosphor-logging (fast!)</span>
devtool build phosphor-logging

<span class="c"># Build output goes to the normal deploy directory</span>
<span class="c"># tmp/work/*/phosphor-logging/*/image/</span>
```

</div></div>

This builds only the modified recipe and its direct dependencies—typically completing in 1-2 minutes instead of 30+.

### devtool reset - Discard Changes

    

When you want to abandon workspace changes and restore the original recipe:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Discard workspace changes for phosphor-logging</span>
devtool reset phosphor-logging

<span class="c"># Verify it's removed</span>
devtool status
```

</div></div>

`devtool reset` permanently deletes your workspace source directory. Commit any changes you want to keep before running this command.

### devtool finish - Create Patches

    

When you’re satisfied with your changes and want to create a permanent patch:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Commit your changes in the workspace</span>
<span class="nb">cd </span>workspace/sources/phosphor-logging
git add <span class="nt">-A</span>
git commit <span class="nt">-m</span> <span class="s2">"Add debug logging for sensor updates"</span>

<span class="c"># Create bbappend with patches in your layer</span>
devtool finish phosphor-logging meta-my-layer

<span class="c"># This creates:</span>
<span class="c"># meta-my-layer/recipes-phosphor/logging/phosphor-logging_%.bbappend</span>
<span class="c"># meta-my-layer/recipes-phosphor/logging/phosphor-logging/0001-Add-debug-logging.patch</span>
```

</div></div>

### Complete Walkthrough: Modify phosphor-logging

    

Let’s walk through a complete example of adding debug output to phosphor-logging:

**Step 1: Extract source**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="nb">cd </span>openbmc
<span class="nb">.</span> setup ast2600-evb
devtool modify phosphor-logging
```

</div></div>

**Step 2: Make changes**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="nb">cd </span>workspace/sources/phosphor-logging

<span class="c"># Edit a source file (example: add debug log)</span>
<span class="c"># Find the main logging implementation</span>
vi lib/lg2_logger.cpp
```

</div></div>

Add a debug line to verify your changes are working:

<div class="language-cpp highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c1">// Near the top of a frequently-called function</span>
<span class="n">std</span><span class="o">::</span><span class="n">cerr</span> <span class="o"><<</span> <span class="s">"DEBUG: phosphor-logging modified successfully</span><span class="se">\n</span><span class="s">"</span><span class="p">;</span>
```

</div></div>

**Step 3: Build**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
devtool build phosphor-logging
```

</div></div>

**Step 4: Deploy and test on QEMU**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Build image with your changes</span>
bitbake obmc-phosphor-image

<span class="c"># Start QEMU (requires QEMU 6.0+)</span>
qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">-m</span> 1G <span class="nt">-M</span> ast2600-evb <span class="nt">-nographic</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-drive</span> <span class="nv">file</span><span class="o">=</span>tmp/deploy/images/ast2600-evb/obmc-phosphor-image-ast2600-evb.static.mtd,format<span class="o">=</span>raw,if<span class="o">=</span>mtd <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-net</span> nic <span class="nt">-net</span> user,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>tcp::2222-:22,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>tcp::2443-:443

<span class="c"># In another terminal, check logs</span>
ssh <span class="nt">-p</span> 2222 root@localhost
journalctl <span class="nt">-f</span> | <span class="nb">grep </span>DEBUG
```

</div></div>

**Step 5: Finalize or reset**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># If satisfied, create permanent patch:</span>
<span class="nb">cd </span>workspace/sources/phosphor-logging
git add <span class="nt">-A</span> <span class="o">&&</span> git commit <span class="nt">-m</span> <span class="s2">"Add debug logging"</span>
devtool finish phosphor-logging meta-my-layer

<span class="c"># Or discard changes:</span>
devtool reset phosphor-logging
```

</div></div>
---

## Recipe Customization with bbappend

    

For permanent, maintainable recipe customizations, use bbappend files instead of modifying upstream recipes directly.

### bbappend Naming Conventions

    

bbappend files must match the recipe name exactly:

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
Recipe:  meta-phosphor/recipes-phosphor/logging/phosphor-logging_git.bb
Append:  meta-my-layer/recipes-phosphor/logging/phosphor-logging_%.bbappend
```

</div></div>

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Pattern | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `recipe_git.bbappend` | Only `recipe_git.bb` |
| `recipe_%.bbappend` | Any version of recipe (recommended) |
| `recipe_1.0.bbappend` | Only version 1.0 |

</div>

### bbappend Directory Structure

    

Your bbappend should mirror the original recipe’s path:

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
meta-your-layer/
└── recipes-phosphor/
    └── logging/
        ├── phosphor-logging_%.bbappend
        └── phosphor-logging/
            ├── 0001-your-patch.patch
            └── your-config-file.conf
```

</div></div>

### Common bbappend Use Cases

    

**Adding patches:**

```bitbake
# phosphor-logging_%.bbappend
FILESEXTRAPATHS:prepend := "${THISDIR}/${PN}:"

SRC_URI += "file://0001-Add-custom-logging.patch"
```

**Modifying SRCREV (pin to specific commit):**

```bitbake
# phosphor-logging_%.bbappend
SRCREV = "abc123def456..."
```

**Adding dependencies:**

```bitbake
# phosphor-logging_%.bbappend
DEPENDS += "additional-library"
RDEPENDS:${PN} += "runtime-dependency"
```

**Modifying configuration options:**

```bitbake
# phosphor-logging_%.bbappend
EXTRA_OEMESON += "-Doption=value"
```

**Adding extra files to the image:**

```bitbake
# phosphor-logging_%.bbappend
FILESEXTRAPATHS:prepend := "${THISDIR}/${PN}:"

SRC_URI += "file://custom.conf"

do_install:append() {
    install -d ${D}${sysconfdir}
    install -m 0644 ${WORKDIR}/custom.conf ${D}${sysconfdir}/
}
```

### Layer Priority

    

When multiple layers have bbappend files for the same recipe, priority determines which applies last (highest priority wins for conflicts):

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Check layer priorities</span>
bitbake-layers show-layers

<span class="c"># Example output:</span>
<span class="c"># layer                 path                                      priority</span>
<span class="c"># meta                  /path/to/poky/meta                        5</span>
<span class="c"># meta-phosphor         /path/to/openbmc/meta-phosphor            7</span>
<span class="c"># meta-my-layer          /path/to/openbmc/meta-my-layer             10</span>
```

</div></div>

Higher priority layers’ appends are processed last. Set priority in your layer’s `conf/layer.conf`:

```bitbake
BBFILE_PRIORITY_meta-yourlayer = "10"
```

### When to Upstream vs Maintain Local Patches

    

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Situation | Recommendation |
| --- | --- |
| Bug fix that benefits everyone | Upstream to OpenBMC |
| Platform-specific hardware support | Keep in machine layer |
| Temporary debug code | Use devtool, don’t commit |
| Feature that may be rejected upstream | Start with bbappend, propose upstream |

</div>

Maintaining local patches creates technical debt. Whenever possible, contribute fixes upstream and remove your bbappend once the fix is merged.

---

## Build Optimization

    

Speed up your builds with caching and parallelization.

### Enable ccache

    

ccache caches compiled objects, dramatically speeding up C/C++ recompilation:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Add to conf/local.conf</span>
INHERIT +<span class="o">=</span> <span class="s2">"ccache"</span>
CCACHE_DIR <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">TOPDIR</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">/ccache"</span>
```

</div></div>

Expected improvement: **2-3x faster** C/C++ compilation on rebuilds.

Verify ccache is working:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># After a build, check cache statistics</span>
ccache <span class="nt">-s</span>

<span class="c"># Look for "cache hit" entries</span>
```

</div></div>

### Configure sstate Cache

    

sstate (shared state) cache stores built recipe outputs, skipping rebuilds for unchanged recipes:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Default location (already configured)</span>
SSTATE_DIR <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">TOPDIR</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">/sstate-cache"</span>

<span class="c"># Share sstate between multiple build directories</span>
SSTATE_DIR <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s2">"/opt/openbmc-sstate"</span>

<span class="c"># Use a read-only shared sstate mirror</span>
SSTATE_MIRRORS <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s2">"file://.* file:///shared/sstate/PATH"</span>
```

</div></div>

sstate cache can grow large (50GB+). Periodically clean old entries with `sstate-cache-management.sh`.

### Parallel Build Configuration

    

Maximize CPU utilization during builds:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Add to conf/local.conf</span>

<span class="c"># Number of parallel BitBake tasks (recipe-level parallelism)</span>
<span class="c"># Recommended: Number of CPU cores</span>
BB_NUMBER_THREADS <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s2">"8"</span>

<span class="c"># Number of parallel make jobs (within each recipe)</span>
<span class="c"># Recommended: Number of CPU cores</span>
PARALLEL_MAKE <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s2">"-j 8"</span>
```

</div></div>

**Formula for your system:**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Check your CPU cores</span>
<span class="nb">nproc</span>

<span class="c"># Set both values to this number (or slightly less to leave headroom)</span>
<span class="c"># For 8-core system:</span>
BB_NUMBER_THREADS <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s2">"8"</span>
PARALLEL_MAKE <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s2">"-j 8"</span>

<span class="c"># For memory-constrained systems (< 32GB RAM), reduce values:</span>
BB_NUMBER_THREADS <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s2">"4"</span>
PARALLEL_MAKE <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s2">"-j 4"</span>
```

</div></div>

### Verify Optimization is Working

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Check ccache hit rate</span>
ccache <span class="nt">-s</span> | <span class="nb">grep</span> <span class="s2">"cache hit"</span>

<span class="c"># Check sstate usage during build (look for "sstate" messages)</span>
bitbake phosphor-logging <span class="nt">-v</span> 2>&1 | <span class="nb">grep</span> <span class="nt">-i</span> sstate

<span class="c"># Monitor parallel jobs</span>
htop  <span class="c"># Watch CPU usage during build</span>
```

</div></div>
---

## Troubleshooting

    

### devtool Workspace Conflicts

    

**Error:** “Recipe is already in your workspace”

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Check what's in your workspace</span>
devtool status

<span class="c"># Reset the conflicting recipe</span>
devtool reset phosphor-logging

<span class="c"># Try again</span>
devtool modify phosphor-logging
```

</div></div>

**Error:** “Workspace directory already exists”

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Remove stale workspace manually</span>
<span class="nb">rm</span> <span class="nt">-rf</span> workspace/sources/phosphor-logging
<span class="nb">rm</span> <span class="nt">-f</span> workspace/appends/phosphor-logging.bbappend

<span class="c"># Try again</span>
devtool modify phosphor-logging
```

</div></div>

### sstate Cache Misses

    

**Symptom:** Full rebuilds despite having sstate cache

Common causes:

1. **SRCREV changed** - Recipe source updated upstream
    
```
# Check current vs cached SRCREV
bitbake -e phosphor-logging | grep ^SRCREV=
```
2. **Configuration drift** - local.conf changes affect recipe hash
    
```
# Compare build signatures
bitbake-diffsigs tmp/stamps/*/phosphor-logging/*/do_compile.*
```
3. **Compiler or host tool version changed**
    
```
# Check for host contamination warnings
bitbake phosphor-logging 2>&1 | grep -i contamination
```

### Workspace Inspection Commands

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># List all recipes in workspace</span>
devtool status

<span class="c"># Show details for a specific recipe</span>
devtool status phosphor-logging

<span class="c"># Find workspace source directory</span>
<span class="nb">ls</span> <span class="nt">-la</span> workspace/sources/

<span class="c"># Check git status of workspace source</span>
<span class="nb">cd </span>workspace/sources/phosphor-logging
git status
git log <span class="nt">--oneline</span> <span class="nt">-5</span>
```

</div></div>

<div id="main-content" class="main-content">
        <main>
          
            
# Building QEMU for OpenBMC

    

Build QEMU from source when your distribution’s package lacks ast2600-evb support.

</li>
  <li><a href="#option-1-use-openbmcs-built-in-qemu-recommended" id="markdown-toc-option-1-use-openbmcs-built-in-qemu-recommended">Option 1: Use OpenBMC’s Built-in QEMU (Recommended)</a>    
1. [Build QEMU via BitBake](#build-qemu-via-bitbake)
2. [Use the Built QEMU](#use-the-built-qemu)

## When You Need This Guide

    

Stock QEMU from Linux distribution package managers often **lacks ASPEED machine support**:

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Distribution | Package QEMU Version | ast2600-evb Support |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ubuntu 20.04 | QEMU 4.2 | ❌ No |
| Ubuntu 22.04 | QEMU 6.2 | ⚠️ Partial |
| Ubuntu 24.04 | QEMU 8.2 | ✅ Yes |
| Fedora 38+ | QEMU 7.2+ | ✅ Yes |
| Debian 11 | QEMU 5.2 | ❌ No |
| Debian 12 | QEMU 7.2 | ✅ Yes |

</div>

### Check Your QEMU Version

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Check version</span>
qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">--version</span>

<span class="c"># Check if ast2600-evb is available</span>
qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">-machine</span> <span class="nb">help</span> | <span class="nb">grep </span>ast2600
```

</div></div>

If `ast2600-evb` is not listed, you need to build QEMU from source.

---

## Option 1: Use OpenBMC’s Built-in QEMU (Recommended)

    

The OpenBMC build system includes a QEMU recipe with full ASPEED support. This is the easiest option.

### Build QEMU via BitBake

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="nb">cd </span>openbmc

<span class="c"># Initialize environment (if not already done)</span>
<span class="nb">.</span> setup ast2600-evb

<span class="c"># Build QEMU native tool</span>
bitbake qemu-system-native

<span class="c"># Find the built QEMU</span>
<span class="nb">ls </span>tmp/work/x86_64-linux/qemu-system-native/<span class="k">*</span>/image/usr/bin/qemu-system-arm
```

</div></div>

### Use the Built QEMU

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Set path to OpenBMC's QEMU</span>
<span class="nv">QEMU_PATH</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s2">"tmp/work/x86_64-linux/qemu-system-native/*/image/usr/bin"</span>

<span class="c"># Run with OpenBMC's QEMU</span>
<span class="nv">$QEMU_PATH</span>/qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">-m</span> 1G <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-M</span> ast2600-evb <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-nographic</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-drive</span> <span class="nv">file</span><span class="o">=</span>tmp/deploy/images/ast2600-evb/obmc-phosphor-image-ast2600-evb.static.mtd,format<span class="o">=</span>raw,if<span class="o">=</span>mtd <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-net</span> nic <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-net</span> user,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>tcp::2222-:22,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>tcp::2443-:443,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>udp::2623-:623
```

</div></div>

### Create a Convenience Script

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c">#!/bin/bash</span>
<span class="c"># save as: run-qemu.sh</span>

<span class="nv">OPENBMC_DIR</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">OPENBMC_DIR</span><span class="k">:-</span><span class="si">$(</span><span class="nb">pwd</span><span class="si">)</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">"</span>
<span class="nv">QEMU</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="si">$(</span>find <span class="nv">$OPENBMC_DIR</span>/tmp/work/x86_64-linux/qemu-system-native <span class="nt">-name</span> qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">-type</span> f | <span class="nb">head</span> <span class="nt">-1</span><span class="si">)</span>
<span class="nv">IMAGE</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s2">"</span><span class="nv">$OPENBMC_DIR</span><span class="s2">/tmp/deploy/images/ast2600-evb/obmc-phosphor-image-ast2600-evb.static.mtd"</span>

<span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">[</span> <span class="o">!</span> <span class="nt">-f</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="nv">$QEMU</span><span class="s2">"</span> <span class="o">]</span><span class="p">;</span> <span class="k">then
    </span><span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"Error: QEMU not found. Run 'bitbake qemu-system-native' first."</span>
    <span class="nb">exit </span>1
<span class="k">fi</span>

<span class="nv">$QEMU</span> <span class="nt">-m</span> 1G <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-M</span> ast2600-evb <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-nographic</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-drive</span> <span class="nv">file</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="nv">$IMAGE</span>,format<span class="o">=</span>raw,if<span class="o">=</span>mtd <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-net</span> nic <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-net</span> user,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>tcp::2222-:22,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>tcp::2443-:443,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>udp::2623-:623
```

</div></div>
---

## Option 2: Build QEMU from Source

    

Build QEMU directly from upstream source for use outside the OpenBMC build environment.

### Install Build Dependencies

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Ubuntu/Debian</span>
<span class="nb">sudo </span>apt update
<span class="nb">sudo </span>apt <span class="nb">install</span> <span class="nt">-y</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    git <span class="se">\</span>
    build-essential <span class="se">\</span>
    ninja-build <span class="se">\</span>
    pkg-config <span class="se">\</span>
    libglib2.0-dev <span class="se">\</span>
    libpixman-1-dev <span class="se">\</span>
    libslirp-dev <span class="se">\</span>
    python3 <span class="se">\</span>
    python3-venv

<span class="c"># Fedora</span>
<span class="nb">sudo </span>dnf <span class="nb">install</span> <span class="nt">-y</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    git <span class="se">\</span>
    gcc <span class="se">\</span>
    g++ <span class="se">\</span>
    ninja-build <span class="se">\</span>
    glib2-devel <span class="se">\</span>
    pixman-devel <span class="se">\</span>
    libslirp-devel <span class="se">\</span>
    python3
```

</div></div>

### Clone and Build QEMU

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Clone QEMU (use version 8.0+ for best ASPEED support)</span>
git clone https://github.com/qemu/qemu.git
<span class="nb">cd </span>qemu
git checkout v8.2.0  <span class="c"># or latest stable</span>

<span class="c"># Configure for ARM system emulation only (faster build)</span>
./configure <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--target-list</span><span class="o">=</span>arm-softmmu <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--enable-slirp</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--disable-docs</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--disable-werror</span>

<span class="c"># Build (use -j for parallel compilation)</span>
make <span class="nt">-j</span><span class="si">$(</span><span class="nb">nproc</span><span class="si">)</span>

<span class="c"># Verify ast2600-evb is available</span>
./build/qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">-machine</span> <span class="nb">help</span> | <span class="nb">grep </span>ast2600
```

</div></div>

### Install System-Wide (Optional)

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Install to /usr/local</span>
<span class="nb">sudo </span>make <span class="nb">install</span>

<span class="c"># Verify installation</span>
qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">--version</span>
qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">-machine</span> <span class="nb">help</span> | <span class="nb">grep </span>ast2600
```

</div></div>

### Install to Custom Location

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Install to home directory</span>
./configure <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--target-list</span><span class="o">=</span>arm-softmmu <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--prefix</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="nv">$HOME</span>/qemu <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--enable-slirp</span>

make <span class="nt">-j</span><span class="si">$(</span><span class="nb">nproc</span><span class="si">)</span>
make <span class="nb">install</span>

<span class="c"># Add to PATH</span>
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s1">'export PATH="$HOME/qemu/bin:$PATH"'</span> <span class="o">>></span> ~/.bashrc
<span class="nb">source</span> ~/.bashrc
```

</div></div>
---

## Option 3: Use Container with QEMU

    

Run QEMU inside a container that has proper ASPEED support.

### Docker with QEMU

    

<div class="language-dockerfile highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Dockerfile.qemu</span>
<span class="k">FROM</span><span class="s"> ubuntu:24.04</span>

<span class="k">RUN </span>apt-get update <span class="o">&&</span> apt-get <span class="nb">install</span> <span class="nt">-y</span> <span class="se">\
</span>    qemu-system-arm <span class="se">\
</span>    <span class="o">&&</span> <span class="nb">rm</span> <span class="nt">-rf</span> /var/lib/apt/lists/<span class="k">*</span>

<span class="k">WORKDIR</span><span class="s"> /openbmc</span>
```

</div></div>

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Build container</span>
docker build <span class="nt">-t</span> openbmc-qemu <span class="nt">-f</span> Dockerfile.qemu <span class="nb">.</span>

<span class="c"># Run QEMU in container (mount image directory)</span>
docker run <span class="nt">-it</span> <span class="nt">--rm</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-v</span> <span class="si">$(</span><span class="nb">pwd</span><span class="si">)</span>/tmp/deploy/images:/images <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-p</span> 2222:2222 <span class="nt">-p</span> 2443:2443 <span class="nt">-p</span> 2623:2623/udp <span class="se">\</span>
    openbmc-qemu <span class="se">\</span>
    qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">-m</span> 1G <span class="nt">-M</span> ast2600-evb <span class="nt">-nographic</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-drive</span> <span class="nv">file</span><span class="o">=</span>/images/ast2600-evb/obmc-phosphor-image-ast2600-evb.static.mtd,format<span class="o">=</span>raw,if<span class="o">=</span>mtd <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-net</span> nic <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-net</span> user,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>tcp::2222-:22,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>tcp::2443-:443,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>udp::2623-:623
```

</div></div>

<span class="c"># List all ASPEED machines</span>
qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">-machine</span> <span class="nb">help</span> | <span class="nb">grep</span> <span class="nt">-i</span> aspeed

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Quick test (will fail without image, but confirms QEMU works)</span>
qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">-M</span> ast2600-evb <span class="nt">-nographic</span> <span class="nt">-serial</span> null
<span class="c"># Press Ctrl+A, X to exit</span>
```

## Machine Selection Reference

    

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Machine | SoC | CPU | Memory | Use Case |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ast2600-evb** | AST2600 | Cortex-A7 (dual) | 1GB | Modern development (recommended) |
| ast2500-evb | AST2500 | ARM926EJ-S | 512MB | Legacy compatibility |
| romulus-bmc | AST2500 | ARM1176 | 256MB | IBM OpenPOWER reference |
| witherspoon-bmc | AST2500 | ARM1176 | 256MB | IBM OpenPOWER reference |

</div>

Use **ast2600-evb** for new development. It has more memory (1GB vs 256MB), a modern CPU, and represents current hardware.

## Troubleshooting

    

### “Machine type not found”

    

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
qemu-system-arm: -M ast2600-evb: unsupported machine type
```

</div></div>

**Solution**: Your QEMU version is too old. Build from source using this guide.

### Build Fails with Missing Dependencies

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Install all possible dependencies</span>
<span class="nb">sudo </span>apt <span class="nb">install</span> <span class="nt">-y</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    libglib2.0-dev libpixman-1-dev libslirp-dev <span class="se">\</span>
    libcap-ng-dev libattr1-dev libaio-dev <span class="se">\</span>
    libnuma-dev libseccomp-dev
```

</div></div>

### Slow Performance

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Enable KVM if running ARM on ARM host</span>
qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">-M</span> ast2600-evb <span class="nt">-enable-kvm</span> ...

<span class="c"># For x86 host, KVM won't help (cross-architecture)</span>
<span class="c"># Allocate more CPU cores</span>
qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">-M</span> ast2600-evb <span class="nt">-smp</span> 2 ...
```

</div></div>
