## Test Execution

    

### Running Tests Against QEMU

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Start QEMU (terminal 1)</span>
qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">-m</span> 1G <span class="nt">-M</span> ast2600-evb <span class="nt">-nographic</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-drive</span> <span class="nv">file</span><span class="o">=</span>obmc-phosphor-image.static.mtd,format<span class="o">=</span>raw,if<span class="o">=</span>mtd <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-net</span> nic <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-net</span> user,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>tcp::2222-:22,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>tcp::2443-:443,hostfwd<span class="o">=</span>udp::2623-:623

<span class="c"># Run tests (terminal 2)</span>
<span class="nb">cd </span>openbmc-test-automation

robot <span class="nt">-v</span> OPENBMC_HOST:localhost <span class="se">\</span>
      <span class="nt">-v</span> SSH_PORT:2222 <span class="se">\</span>
      <span class="nt">-v</span> HTTPS_PORT:2443 <span class="se">\</span>
      <span class="nt">-v</span> OPENBMC_USERNAME:root <span class="se">\</span>
      <span class="nt">-v</span> OPENBMC_PASSWORD:0penBmc <span class="se">\</span>
      redfish/service_root/test_service_root.robot
```

</div></div>

### Running Tests Against Real Hardware

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
robot <span class="nt">-v</span> OPENBMC_HOST:192.168.1.100 <span class="se">\</span>
      <span class="nt">-v</span> SSH_PORT:22 <span class="se">\</span>
      <span class="nt">-v</span> HTTPS_PORT:443 <span class="se">\</span>
      <span class="nt">-v</span> OPENBMC_USERNAME:root <span class="se">\</span>
      <span class="nt">-v</span> OPENBMC_PASSWORD:0penBmc <span class="se">\</span>
      redfish/service_root/test_service_root.robot
```

</div></div>

### Running Specific Test Suites

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Run single test file</span>
robot redfish/account_service/test_accounts.robot

<span class="c"># Run tests with specific tag</span>
robot <span class="nt">--include</span> smoke redfish/

<span class="c"># Run tests excluding a tag</span>
robot <span class="nt">--exclude</span> destructive redfish/

<span class="c"># Run specific test case</span>
robot <span class="nt">--test</span> <span class="s2">"Verify Service Root"</span> redfish/service_root/
```

</div></div>

### Test Output Options

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Custom output directory</span>
robot <span class="nt">-d</span> results/ test_suite.robot

<span class="c"># Custom report name</span>
robot <span class="nt">-r</span> custom_report.html test_suite.robot

<span class="c"># Log level</span>
robot <span class="nt">-L</span> DEBUG test_suite.robot
robot <span class="nt">-L</span> TRACE test_suite.robot
```

</div></div>

### Argument Files (test_lists/)

    

Passing long lists of suites, tags, and variables on the command line gets unwieldy, so the repository ships **Robot argument files** in the `test_lists/` directory. Each file is a curated set of `robot` arguments for one scenario:

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Argument file | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `HW_CI` | Suites safe to run against real hardware in CI |
| `CT_basic_run` | A basic continuous-test smoke run |
| `QEMU_CI` | Suites suitable for QEMU-based CI |
| `skip_test_witherspoon`, `skip_test_palmetto` | Platform-specific skip lists |

</div>

Point `robot` at one with `--argumentfile`:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
robot <span class="nt">--argumentfile</span> test_lists/HW_CI <span class="se">\</span>
      <span class="nt">-v</span> OPENBMC_HOST:192.168.1.100 <span class="se">\</span>
      <span class="nt">-v</span> OPENBMC_USERNAME:root <span class="se">\</span>
      <span class="nt">-v</span> OPENBMC_PASSWORD:0penBmc <span class="se">\</span>
      redfish/
```

</div></div>

You can supply `--argumentfile` more than once – for example, combine a run list with a platform skip list to exclude tests that do not apply to your board.

## First Failure Data Capture (FFDC)

    

When a test fails you usually need the BMC’s logs and state *from the moment of failure* to debug it. `openbmc-test-automation` automates this with **First Failure Data Capture (FFDC)**: on a failed test, a teardown keyword collects logs, journals, dumps, and inventory from the target and saves them alongside the Robot results.

### Collection Plugins

    

FFDC data is gathered by protocol plugins in `ffdc/plugins/`, each of which knows how to pull data over one transport:

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Plugin | Transport | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ssh_execution.py` | SSH | Run commands on the BMC and capture stdout |
| `scp_execution.py` | SCP | Copy log files and dumps off the BMC |
| `telnet_execution.py` | Telnet | Collect data over serial/console-style access |
| `redfish.py` | Redfish | Walk and dump the Redfish resource tree |

</div>

The `redfish.py` plugin uses **`redfishtool`** to recursively enumerate the service: `enumerate_request()` issues `GET` requests and `walk_nested_dict()` follows every `@odata.id` and `Members` link, producing a full JSON snapshot of the tree.

### Wiring FFDC Into a Suite

    

FFDC runs from teardown keywords so it fires automatically on failure. The Robot glue lives in `lib/openbmc_ffdc.robot`, and `lib/ffdc_cli_robot_script.py` drives the plugin-based collector:

<div class="language-robot highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="gh">*** Settings ***</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="bp">Resource</span><span class="w">          </span><span class="nf">../lib/openbmc_ffdc.robot</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="bp">Test Teardown</span><span class="w">     </span><span class="nf">FFDC On Test Case Fail</span><span class="w">

</span><span class="gh">*** Test Cases ***</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="nl">Power On Host</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="p">[</span><span class="bp">Documentation</span><span class="p">]</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">Power on and capture FFDC if the test fails.</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="p">[</span><span class="bp">Tags</span><span class="p">]</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">power</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nf">Redfish Power On</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nf">Wait Until Keyword Succeeds</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">3 min</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">10 sec</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">Is Host Running</span><span class="w">
</span>
```

</div></div>

If `Power On Host` fails, `FFDC On Test Case Fail` collects logs through the plugins above before the suite moves on.

### Plug-in Package Framework

    

> FFDC’s collectors are one use of a more general **plug-in package framework**. `bin/process_plug_in_packages.py` discovers and runs plug-in packages, invoking their *call-point* programs (scripts run at defined points in the test flow, such as setup, cleanup, or FFDC collection), and `bin/validate_plug_ins.py` checks that a package is well-formed. Reusable plug-in packages ship under `bin/plug_ins/`. This lets you extend a run with custom setup, teardown, or data-collection logic without modifying the test suites themselves.

---

## GUI Test Automation

    

Beyond API-level tests, `openbmc-test-automation` drives the OpenBMC web UI end-to-end in a real browser using **SeleniumLibrary**.

### Test Layout

    

The current GUI suites target the Vue-based **webui-vue** front end and live under `gui/gui_test/`, organized by menu (for example `gui/gui_test/operations_menu/` and `gui/gui_test/settings_menu/`). Earlier AngularJS-era GUI tests (for the legacy `phosphor-webui`) have largely been retired as the web UI moved to Vue.

### Locators

    

Rather than scattering XPaths through the tests, element locators are centralized under `gui/data/`:

<div class="table-wrapper">
| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `gui/data/gui_variables.py` | XPath and string constants for the Vue GUI |
| `gui/data/resource_variables.py` | Shared resource locators and identifiers |

</div>

Tests prefer stable **`data-test-id`** attributes rendered by webui-vue, so locators survive cosmetic markup changes.

### Running GUI Tests

    

GUI tests need a Selenium-driven browser and a matching WebDriver (for example ChromeDriver). Setup steps are documented in `docs/gui_setup_reference.md`. A run looks like:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
robot <span class="nt">-v</span> OPENBMC_HOST:<span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">OPENBMC_HOST</span><span class="k">}</span> <span class="se">\</span>
      <span class="nt">-v</span> OPENBMC_USERNAME:root <span class="se">\</span>
      <span class="nt">-v</span> OPENBMC_PASSWORD:0penBmc <span class="se">\</span>
      gui/gui_test/
```

</div></div>

> GUI tests are browser- and timing-sensitive, so they run slower and break more easily than Redfish or IPMI tests. Keep them out of fast smoke runs and gate them behind their own tags or argument file.

---

## Common Test Patterns

    

### Redfish API Test

    

<div class="language-robot highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="gh">*** Settings ***</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="bp">Library</span><span class="w">           </span><span class="nf">RequestsLibrary</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="bp">Library</span><span class="w">           </span><span class="nf">Collections</span><span class="w">

</span><span class="gh">*** Variables ***</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="nv">${REDFISH_BASE}</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">/redfish/v1</span><span class="w">

</span><span class="gh">*** Test Cases ***</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="nl">Get System Information Via Redfish</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="p">[</span><span class="bp">Documentation</span><span class="p">]</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">Retrieve system info via Redfish</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="p">[</span><span class="bp">Tags</span><span class="p">]</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">redfish</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">system</span><span class="w">

    </span><span class="c"># Authenticate</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nv">${auth}</span><span class="nf">=</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">Create List</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="nv">${OPENBMC_USERNAME}</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="nv">${OPENBMC_PASSWORD}</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nf">Create Session</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">bmc</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">https://</span><span class="nv">${OPENBMC_HOST}</span><span class="s">:</span><span class="nv">${HTTPS_PORT}</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nf">...</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">auth=</span><span class="nv">${auth}</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">verify=</span><span class="nv">${False}</span><span class="w">

    </span><span class="c"># Get system resource</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nv">${resp}</span><span class="nf">=</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">GET On Session</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">bmc</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="nv">${REDFISH_BASE}</span><span class="s">/Systems/system</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nf">Should Be Equal As Integers</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="nv">${resp.status_code}</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">200</span><span class="w">

    </span><span class="c"># Verify fields</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nv">${json}</span><span class="nf">=</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">Set Variable</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="nv">${resp.json()}</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nf">Should Be Equal</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="nv">${json["PowerState"]}</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">On</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nf">Should Not Be Empty</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="nv">${json["SerialNumber"]}</span><span class="w">

</span><span class="nl">Patch System Asset Tag</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="p">[</span><span class="bp">Documentation</span><span class="p">]</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">Update system asset tag</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="p">[</span><span class="bp">Tags</span><span class="p">]</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">redfish</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">system</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">patch</span><span class="w">

    </span><span class="nv">${auth}</span><span class="nf">=</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">Create List</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="nv">${OPENBMC_USERNAME}</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="nv">${OPENBMC_PASSWORD}</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nf">Create Session</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">bmc</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">https://</span><span class="nv">${OPENBMC_HOST}</span><span class="s">:</span><span class="nv">${HTTPS_PORT}</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nf">...</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">auth=</span><span class="nv">${auth}</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">verify=</span><span class="nv">${False}</span><span class="w">

    </span><span class="c"># Update asset tag</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nv">${payload}</span><span class="nf">=</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">Create Dictionary</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">AssetTag=TestAsset123</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nv">${headers}</span><span class="nf">=</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">Create Dictionary</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">Content-Type=application/json</span><span class="w">

    </span><span class="nv">${resp}</span><span class="nf">=</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">PATCH On Session</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">bmc</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="nv">${REDFISH_BASE}</span><span class="s">/Systems/system</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nf">...</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">json=</span><span class="nv">${payload}</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">headers=</span><span class="nv">${headers}</span><span class="w">

    </span><span class="nf">Should Be Equal As Integers</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="nv">${resp.status_code}</span><span class="w">    </span><span class="s">200</span><span class="w">
</span>
```

</div></div>

> **Under the hood: `bmc_redfish` and mTLS.** The higher-level Redfish keywords in the suite are backed by `lib/bmc_redfish.py`, whose `bmc_redfish` class extends `redfish_plus` (a thin wrapper over the DMTF `redfish` Python library). Its `enumerate()` keyword recursively walks the service (via `walk_nested_dict()`) to snapshot the whole tree. For mutual-TLS testing, set `MTLS_ENABLED=True` so the client authenticates with a certificate instead of a session token, together with `VALID_CERT` and `CERT_DIR_PATH` (defined in `lib/redfish_plus.py` and `lib/resource.robot`). See `docs/redfish_request_via_mTLS.md` for the full mTLS setup.

## Troubleshooting

    

### Common Issues

    

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Issue | Cause | Solution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connection refused | BMC not running | Start QEMU or check network |
| SSL certificate error | Self-signed cert | Use `verify=${False}` |
| Authentication failed | Wrong credentials | Verify username/password |
| Timeout waiting for host | Slow boot | Increase timeout values |
| IPMI connection failed | Port not forwarded | Check QEMU port forwarding (UDP 623) |

</div>

### Debug Tips

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Run with debug logging</span>
robot <span class="nt">-L</span> DEBUG test.robot

<span class="c"># Trace library calls</span>
robot <span class="nt">-L</span> TRACE test.robot

<span class="c"># Dry run (syntax check)</span>
robot <span class="nt">--dryrun</span> test.robot

<span class="c"># List tests without running</span>
robot <span class="nt">--list</span> test.robot
```

</div></div>

### Checking BMC State

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># SSH to BMC</span>
ssh <span class="nt">-p</span> 2222 root@localhost

<span class="c"># Check service status</span>
systemctl status bmcweb
systemctl status phosphor-ipmi-host

<span class="c"># View logs</span>
journalctl <span class="nt">-u</span> bmcweb <span class="nt">-f</span>
```

## Overview

    

When developing or modifying drivers for OpenBMC, you often need to patch the Linux kernel image itself. Unlike userspace services that live in separate recipes, kernel changes — new drivers, bug fixes, device tree modifications, or configuration changes — require a structured patching workflow through Yocto/BitBake.

OpenBMC maintains its own kernel tree at [openbmc/linux](https://github.com/openbmc/linux) with a development branch naming convention of `dev-X.Y` (e.g., `dev-6.18`). The kernel recipe pins to a specific commit hash for reproducibility, and your patches are applied on top during the build.

**Key concepts covered:**

* How OpenBMC organizes kernel recipes across meta-layers
* Two workflows for kernel patching: `devtool` (interactive) and `bbappend` (permanent)
* Creating and applying kernel configuration fragments
* Device tree patching for new hardware
* Testing kernel changes on QEMU before flashing hardware
* Building out-of-tree kernel modules as standalone Yocto recipes
* Userspace driver alternatives (libgpiod, i2c-dev, spidev, UIO)
* Driver debugging techniques (dynamic_debug, ftrace, debugfs)
* End-to-end I2C/SPI sensor binding walkthrough
* Best practices for upstreaming patches

Kernel patches directly affect system stability. Always test on QEMU before deploying to hardware. A bad kernel patch can brick a BMC, requiring physical recovery.

---

## How OpenBMC Structures Kernel Recipes

    

Understanding the layer hierarchy helps you know where to place your patches.

### Layer Hierarchy

    

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Platform/Vendor Layer  (meta-ibm, meta-google, etc.)   │
│  ── Machine-specific patches + config fragments         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Distribution Layer  (meta-phosphor)                    │
│  ── Phosphor-specific kernel configs (GPIO, etc.)       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  BSP Layer  (meta-aspeed, meta-nuvoton)                 │
│  ── Base kernel recipe, SoC defconfig, kernel source    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

</div></div>

Each layer adds its own `.bbappend` files and config fragments on top of the base recipe. The build system merges them in layer priority order.

### Key Files in meta-aspeed

    

<div class="table-wrapper">
| File | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `recipes-kernel/linux/linux-aspeed_git.bb` | Pins kernel branch, version, and commit hash |
| `recipes-kernel/linux/linux-aspeed.inc` | SRC_URI, license, build settings, conditional features |
| `recipes-kernel/linux/linux-aspeed/aspeed-g4/defconfig` | AST2400 (ARMv5) base kernel config |
| `recipes-kernel/linux/linux-aspeed/aspeed-g5/defconfig` | AST2500 (ARMv6) base kernel config |
| `recipes-kernel/linux/linux-aspeed/aspeed-g6/defconfig` | AST2600 (ARMv7) base kernel config |

</div>

### The Base Kernel Recipe

    

The `linux-aspeed_git.bb` recipe is minimal — it pins the source and delegates to the include:

```bitbake
KBRANCH ?= "dev-6.18"
LINUX_VERSION ?= "6.18.8"
SRCREV = "3fcb5927beef6fc8d9faa16b90c01fc6e67f2065"

require linux-aspeed.inc
```

The include file (`linux-aspeed.inc`) sets up the source fetch, defconfig selection, and conditional features:

```bitbake
KSRC ?= "git://github.com/openbmc/linux;protocol=https;branch=${KBRANCH}"
SRC_URI = "${KSRC}"
SRC_URI += "file://defconfig"

# Conditional: TPM2 support
SRC_URI += "${@bb.utils.contains('MACHINE_FEATURES', 'tpm2', 'file://tpm2.cfg', '', d)}"

# Conditional: UBI filesystem
SRC_URI += "${@bb.utils.contains('DISTRO_FEATURES', 'ubi', 'file://ubi.cfg', '', d)}"

KCONFIG_MODE = "--alldefconfig"
inherit kernel linux-yocto
```

---

## Workflow 1: devtool (Interactive Development)

    

Use `devtool` when you are actively developing a kernel change — editing code, testing iteratively, and refining before committing. This is the recommended workflow for driver development.

### Step-by-Step

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># 1. Source the OpenBMC build environment for your machine</span>
<span class="nb">cd </span>openbmc
<span class="nb">.</span> setup romulus

<span class="c"># 2. Check out the kernel source into a workspace</span>
devtool modify linux-aspeed
```

</div></div>

This clones the kernel into `build/workspace/sources/linux-aspeed/` and sets up BitBake to build from your local checkout instead of the cached source.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># 3. Navigate to the kernel source</span>
<span class="nb">cd </span>build/workspace/sources/linux-aspeed

<span class="c"># 4. Make your driver changes</span>
vim drivers/hwmon/my_sensor.c
vim drivers/hwmon/Makefile
vim drivers/hwmon/Kconfig

<span class="c"># 5. Commit your changes (REQUIRED — uncommitted changes are ignored!)</span>
git add drivers/hwmon/my_sensor.c drivers/hwmon/Makefile drivers/hwmon/Kconfig
git commit <span class="nt">-s</span> <span class="nt">-m</span> <span class="s2">"hwmon: my_sensor: Add support for XYZ sensor chip"</span>
```

</div></div>

You **must** commit your changes to git. The `devtool` workflow ignores uncommitted modifications in the working tree.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># 6. Build just the kernel to test compilation</span>
devtool build linux-aspeed

<span class="c"># 7. Or build the full image</span>
bitbake obmc-phosphor-image

<span class="c"># 8. When satisfied, export patches to your meta-layer</span>
devtool finish linux-aspeed ~/openbmc/meta-mymachine

<span class="c"># OR create just a bbappend without removing the workspace</span>
devtool update-recipe <span class="nt">-a</span> ~/openbmc/meta-mymachine linux-aspeed

<span class="c"># 9. Clean up the workspace when done</span>
devtool reset linux-aspeed
```

</div></div>

### Interactive Kernel Configuration

    

Use `menuconfig` to explore and change kernel options interactively:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Open the ncurses-based config editor</span>
bitbake linux-aspeed <span class="nt">-c</span> menuconfig

<span class="c"># After saving, generate a defconfig</span>
bitbake linux-aspeed <span class="nt">-c</span> savedefconfig
```

</div></div>

The `devtool modify` command checks out the branch specified in the recipe (e.g., `dev-6.18`). Unlike some recipes, it does **not** create a separate `devtool` branch — patches are applied directly on the checked-out branch.

---

## Workflow 2: bbappend with Patch Files (Permanent Integration)

    

Use this approach when you have a finalized patch ready to integrate into your machine layer. This is the standard method for production systems.

### Creating Patch Files

    

Generate patches from your kernel git tree using `git format-patch`:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Single patch from the last commit</span>
git format-patch <span class="nt">-1</span>

<span class="c"># Multiple patches from the last 3 commits</span>
git format-patch <span class="nt">-3</span>

<span class="c"># Patches since branching from a base</span>
git format-patch origin/dev-6.18..HEAD
```

</div></div>

This produces numbered patch files like `0001-hwmon-my_sensor-Add-support-for-XYZ.patch`.

### Directory Structure

    

Place patches in your meta-layer following this convention:

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
meta-vendor/
  meta-platform/
    recipes-kernel/
      linux/
        linux-aspeed_%.bbappend          # The append file
        linux-aspeed/                     # Directory matching recipe name
          my-platform.cfg                 # Config fragment
          0001-hwmon-add-xyz-driver.patch # Kernel source patch
          0002-dts-add-platform.patch     # Device tree patch
```

</div></div>

### Writing the bbappend

    

Create `linux-aspeed_%.bbappend` (the `%` wildcard matches any version):

```bitbake
FILESEXTRAPATHS:prepend := "${THISDIR}/${PN}:"

SRC_URI += " \
    file://0001-hwmon-add-xyz-driver.patch \
    file://0002-dts-add-platform.patch \
    file://my-platform.cfg \
"
```

The `FILESEXTRAPATHS:prepend` line tells BitBake to search the `linux-aspeed/` subdirectory (matching `${PN}`) alongside the append file for the referenced files.

### Real-World Example: Vesnin Platform

    

From `meta-yadro/meta-vesnin`:

```bitbake
FILESEXTRAPATHS:prepend := "${THISDIR}/${PN}:"
SRC_URI:append:vesnin = " \
    file://vesnin.cfg \
    file://0002-vesnin-remap-aspeed-uart.patch \
"
```

This adds a UART remapping patch and a platform-specific config fragment, but only for the `vesnin` machine.

### Patch Application Order

    

Patches listed in `SRC_URI` with `file://` are **not guaranteed** to apply in the order listed. To enforce ordering, use a `.scc` (Series Configuration Control) file:

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
# my-patches.scc
patch 0001-first-fix.patch
patch 0002-second-fix.patch
patch 0003-third-fix.patch
```

</div></div>

Then reference the `.scc` file in `SRC_URI` instead of individual patches.

---

## Kernel Configuration Fragments

    

Rather than maintaining a complete defconfig (thousands of lines), use **configuration fragments** — small `.cfg` files containing only the options you need to change.

### Creating Fragments

    

**Method 1: diffconfig (recommended)**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Start from a clean config</span>
bitbake linux-aspeed <span class="nt">-c</span> kernel_configme <span class="nt">-f</span>

<span class="c"># Make changes interactively</span>
bitbake linux-aspeed <span class="nt">-c</span> menuconfig

<span class="c"># Generate a fragment of just your changes</span>
bitbake linux-aspeed <span class="nt">-c</span> diffconfig
<span class="c"># Output: fragment.cfg in the kernel work directory</span>
```

</div></div>

**Method 2: Manual creation**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="nb">cat</span> <span class="o">></span> my-driver.cfg <span class="o"><<</span> <span class="sh">'</span><span class="no">EOF</span><span class="sh">'
CONFIG_I2C_SLAVE=y
CONFIG_SENSORS_LM75=y
CONFIG_SENSORS_TMP421=m
# CONFIG_SENSORS_FAKE is not set
</span><span class="no">EOF
</span>
```

</div></div>

### Applying Fragments

    

Add the fragment via your `.bbappend`:

```bitbake
FILESEXTRAPATHS:prepend := "${THISDIR}/${PN}:"
SRC_URI += "file://my-driver.cfg"
```

### Validating Configuration

    

Verify that all fragment options were applied correctly:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
bitbake linux-aspeed <span class="nt">-c</span> kernel_configcheck <span class="nt">-f</span>
```

</div></div>

This produces warnings when a requested option does not appear in the final `.config`, helping you catch silent configuration failures.

Start `.cfg` files with a blank line — some Yocto versions silently skip the first line. The `KCONFIG_MODE = "--alldefconfig"` setting in `linux-aspeed.inc` means any option not explicitly set gets its default value.

---

## Device Tree Patching

    

Device trees describe hardware to the kernel. For a new platform or hardware modification, you often need to add or patch a device tree source (DTS) file.

### DTS Naming Convention

    

OpenBMC follows the upstream Linux convention:

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
aspeed-bmc-<vendor>-
.dts
```

Examples: `aspeed-bmc-opp-romulus.dts`, `aspeed-bmc-ibm-rainier.dts`, `aspeed-bmc-amd-onyx.dts`

All DTS files live in `arch/arm/boot/dts/aspeed/` in the kernel tree and include base SoC definitions:

<div class="table-wrapper">
| SoC | Include | Generation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AST2400 | `aspeed-g4.dtsi` | G4 (ARMv5) |
| AST2500 | `aspeed-g5.dtsi` | G5 (ARMv6) |
| AST2600 | `aspeed-g6.dtsi` | G6 (ARMv7) |

</div>

### Creating a New Device Tree

    

```dts
// SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0-or-later
// aspeed-bmc-vendor-platform.dts
/dts-v1/;

#include "aspeed-g6.dtsi"
#include <dt-bindings/gpio/aspeed-gpio.h>
#include <dt-bindings/leds/common.h>

/ {
    model = "Vendor Platform BMC";
    compatible = "vendor,platform-bmc", "aspeed,ast2600";

    chosen {
        stdout-path = &uart5;
        bootargs = "console=ttyS4,115200n8 root=/dev/ram rw";
    };

    leds {
        compatible = "gpio-leds";
        fault {
            gpios = <&gpio ASPEED_GPIO(N, 2) GPIO_ACTIVE_LOW>;
        };
    };
};

&i2c0 {
    status = "okay";

    temperature-sensor@48 {
        compatible = "ti,tmp175";
        reg = <0x48>;
    };
};

&uart5 {
    status = "okay";
};
```

### Adding DTS to the Build

    

Two files need changes:

1. Add to the kernel Makefile (`arch/arm/boot/dts/aspeed/Makefile`):
    
```
dtb-$(CONFIG_ARCH_ASPEED) += aspeed-bmc-vendor-platform.dtb
```
2. Set in your machine configuration:
    
```bitbake
KERNEL_DEVICETREE = "aspeed-bmc-vendor-platform.dtb"
```

### Patching an Existing Device Tree

    

Generate a patch, then add it via `.bbappend`:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># In the kernel tree</span>
git add <span class="nb">arch</span>/arm/boot/dts/aspeed/aspeed-bmc-vendor-platform.dts
git add <span class="nb">arch</span>/arm/boot/dts/aspeed/Makefile
git commit <span class="nt">-s</span> <span class="nt">-m</span> <span class="s2">"ARM: dts: aspeed: Add Vendor Platform BMC device tree"</span>
git format-patch <span class="nt">-1</span>
```

</div></div>

```bitbake
# linux-aspeed_%.bbappend
FILESEXTRAPATHS:prepend := "${THISDIR}/${PN}:"
SRC_URI += "file://0001-ARM-dts-aspeed-Add-Vendor-Platform-BMC-device-tree.patch"
```

Device tree source files are an **exception** to the upstream-first rule in OpenBMC. You can carry DTS patches in your meta-layer without waiting for upstream acceptance. However, you should still aim to upstream them eventually.

---

## Testing Kernel Changes

    

### QEMU Testing

    

Always validate kernel patches on QEMU before deploying to hardware:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Build the full image with your kernel changes</span>
bitbake obmc-phosphor-image

<span class="c"># Boot with QEMU</span>
qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">-M</span> ast2600-evb <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-drive</span> <span class="nv">file</span><span class="o">=</span>tmp/deploy/images/ast2600-evb/flash-ast2600-evb,format<span class="o">=</span>raw,if<span class="o">=</span>mtd <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-nographic</span>
```

</div></div>

Or boot kernel and DTB separately:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
qemu-system-arm <span class="nt">-M</span> ast2600-evb <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-kernel</span> tmp/deploy/images/ast2600-evb/zImage <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-dtb</span> tmp/deploy/images/ast2600-evb/aspeed-bmc-vendor-platform.dtb <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-initrd</span> tmp/deploy/images/ast2600-evb/obmc-phosphor-initramfs-ast2600-evb.cpio.gz <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-nographic</span>
```

</div></div>

### TFTP Netboot (Without Reflashing)

    

For faster iteration, serve the kernel image over TFTP instead of reflashing:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Copy FIT image to TFTP server</span>
<span class="nb">cp </span>tmp/deploy/images/<machine>/fitImage /tftpboot/

<span class="c"># In U-Boot console on the BMC:</span>
setenv ipaddr 192.168.0.80
setenv serverip 192.168.0.11
tftp 0x83000000 fitImage
bootm 0x83000000
```

</div></div>

Use `0x43000000` for AST2400 boards. Use `0x83000000` for AST2500/AST2600. This address is the kernel load address in DRAM.

### Out-of-Tree Kernel Build

    

For the fastest compile-test cycle, build the kernel outside of BitBake entirely:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Configure for AST2600</span>
make <span class="nv">ARCH</span><span class="o">=</span>arm <span class="nv">O</span><span class="o">=</span>obj <span class="nv">CROSS_COMPILE</span><span class="o">=</span>arm-linux-gnueabihf- aspeed_g6_defconfig

<span class="c"># Build</span>
make <span class="nv">ARCH</span><span class="o">=</span>arm <span class="nv">O</span><span class="o">=</span>obj <span class="nv">CROSS_COMPILE</span><span class="o">=</span>arm-linux-gnueabihf- <span class="nt">-j</span><span class="si">$(</span><span class="nb">nproc</span><span class="si">)</span>

<span class="c"># Build with initramfs baked in</span>
make <span class="nv">ARCH</span><span class="o">=</span>arm <span class="nv">O</span><span class="o">=</span>obj <span class="nv">CROSS_COMPILE</span><span class="o">=</span>arm-linux-gnueabihf- <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nv">CONFIG_INITRAMFS_SOURCE</span><span class="o">=</span>/path/to/obmc-phosphor-image-<machine>.cpio.gz
```

</div></div>

The cross-compiler (`arm-linux-gnueabihf-`) is available from your Yocto SDK or your distribution’s `gcc-arm-linux-gnueabihf` package.

---

## Verifying Your Patches

    

After building, verify that your changes took effect.

### Check Kernel Version and Patches

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># On the running BMC</span>
<span class="nb">uname</span> <span class="nt">-a</span>
<span class="nb">cat</span> /proc/version
```

</div></div>

### Verify Driver is Loaded

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Check if your driver module is loaded</span>
lsmod | <span class="nb">grep </span>my_driver

<span class="c"># Check kernel ring buffer for driver messages</span>
dmesg | <span class="nb">grep </span>my_driver

<span class="c"># Check device tree nodes</span>
<span class="nb">ls</span> /proc/device-tree/
<span class="nb">cat</span> /proc/device-tree/compatible
```

</div></div>

### Verify Kernel Config

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># If /proc/config.gz is enabled</span>
zcat /proc/config.gz | <span class="nb">grep </span>CONFIG_MY_OPTION
```

</div></div>

### BitBake Validation

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Verify config fragments were applied</span>
bitbake linux-aspeed <span class="nt">-c</span> kernel_configcheck <span class="nt">-f</span>

<span class="c"># Verify patch application succeeded</span>
bitbake linux-aspeed <span class="nt">-c</span> patch
```

</div></div>
---

## Common Patch Scenarios

    

### Scenario 1: Adding a New hwmon Driver

    

A new temperature sensor on the I2C bus needs a kernel driver.

1. Add driver source to `drivers/hwmon/` and update `Kconfig`/`Makefile`
2. Add the device node to your platform DTS
3. Create a config fragment enabling the driver
4. Package as patches in your meta-layer

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
meta-vendor/recipes-kernel/linux/
  linux-aspeed_%.bbappend
  linux-aspeed/
    0001-hwmon-add-xyz-sensor-driver.patch     # Driver code
    0002-dts-add-xyz-sensor-to-platform.patch   # DTS node
    enable-xyz-sensor.cfg                       # CONFIG_SENSORS_XYZ=y
```

</div></div>

### Scenario 2: Fixing an Existing Driver Bug

    

A known upstream fix hasn’t been backported to the OpenBMC kernel branch yet.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Cherry-pick from upstream Linux</span>
<span class="nb">cd </span>build/workspace/sources/linux-aspeed
git cherry-pick <upstream-commit-hash>

<span class="c"># If it doesn't apply cleanly, resolve conflicts and commit</span>
git add <span class="nt">-u</span>
git commit <span class="nt">-s</span>

<span class="c"># Export the patch</span>
git format-patch <span class="nt">-1</span>
```

</div></div>

### Scenario 3: Enabling a Kernel Subsystem

    

You need USB gadget support that is disabled by default.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Create a config fragment</span>
<span class="nb">cat</span> <span class="o">></span> usb-gadget.cfg <span class="o"><<</span> <span class="sh">'</span><span class="no">EOF</span><span class="sh">'

CONFIG_USB_GADGET=y
CONFIG_USB_CONFIGFS=y
CONFIG_USB_CONFIGFS_MASS_STORAGE=y
</span><span class="no">EOF
</span>
```

</div></div>

No kernel source patches needed — just the `.cfg` fragment and a `.bbappend`.

---

## Out-of-Tree Kernel Modules

    

When your driver does not belong in the upstream kernel tree — vendor-specific hardware, proprietary logic, or rapid prototyping — build it as an **out-of-tree kernel module**. This keeps your driver in its own Yocto recipe, decoupled from the kernel source and build cycle.

### When to Use Out-of-Tree vs In-Tree

    

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Factor | Out-of-Tree Module | In-Tree Patch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Upstream acceptance | Not planned or not possible | Planned or already accepted |
| Build coupling | Independent recipe, faster rebuilds | Tied to full kernel rebuild |
| Development speed | Fast iteration — rebuild only your module | Slower — full kernel compile on change |
| Kernel API stability | Must track API changes across kernel versions | Automatically consistent |
| Deployment | Can be updated independently of kernel | Requires full firmware image update |

</div>

For most BMC production drivers, prefer in-tree patches (upstream-first policy). Use out-of-tree modules for vendor-specific hardware abstraction layers, debug/test modules, or drivers still in active prototyping.

### Recipe Layout in Your Meta-Layer

    

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
meta-vendor/
  meta-platform/
    recipes-kernel/
      my-hwmon-module/
        my-hwmon-module_1.0.bb           # Yocto recipe
        files/
          Makefile                         # Kbuild Makefile
          my_hwmon_driver.c               # Module source
          my-hwmon-module.conf            # Autoload config
```

</div></div>

### Kbuild Makefile

    

The out-of-tree module Makefile uses standard Kbuild syntax:

<div class="language-makefile highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># files/Makefile
</span><span class="nv">obj-m</span> <span class="o">:=</span> my_hwmon_driver.o
```

</div></div>

For multi-file modules:

<div class="language-makefile highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="nv">obj-m</span> <span class="o">:=</span> my_hwmon_driver.o
<span class="nv">my_hwmon_driver-objs</span> <span class="o">:=</span> main.o i2c_ops.o sysfs_attrs.o
```

</div></div>

### Module Source (Minimal Example)

    

<div class="language-c highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c1">// files/my_hwmon_driver.c</span>
<span class="cp">#include</span> <span class="cpf"><linux/module.h></span><span class="cp">
#include</span> <span class="cpf"><linux/i2c.h></span><span class="cp">
#include</span> <span class="cpf"><linux/hwmon.h></span><span class="cp">
</span>
<span class="k">static</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="nf">my_hwmon_probe</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">struct</span> <span class="n">i2c_client</span> <span class="o">*</span><span class="n">client</span><span class="p">)</span>
<span class="p">{</span>
    <span class="n">dev_info</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="o">&</span><span class="n">client</span><span class="o">-></span><span class="n">dev</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="s">"my_hwmon_driver probed at 0x%02x</span><span class="se">\n</span><span class="s">"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">client</span><span class="o">-></span><span class="n">addr</span><span class="p">);</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">;</span>
<span class="p">}</span>

<span class="k">static</span> <span class="k">const</span> <span class="k">struct</span> <span class="n">of_device_id</span> <span class="n">my_hwmon_of_match</span><span class="p">[]</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">{</span>
    <span class="p">{</span> <span class="p">.</span><span class="n">compatible</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">"vendor,my-sensor"</span> <span class="p">},</span>
    <span class="p">{</span> <span class="p">}</span>
<span class="p">};</span>
<span class="n">MODULE_DEVICE_TABLE</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">of</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">my_hwmon_of_match</span><span class="p">);</span>

<span class="k">static</span> <span class="k">struct</span> <span class="n">i2c_driver</span> <span class="n">my_hwmon_driver</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">{</span>
    <span class="p">.</span><span class="n">driver</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">{</span>
        <span class="p">.</span><span class="n">name</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">"my-hwmon-driver"</span><span class="p">,</span>
        <span class="p">.</span><span class="n">of_match_table</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">my_hwmon_of_match</span><span class="p">,</span>
    <span class="p">},</span>
    <span class="p">.</span><span class="n">probe</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">my_hwmon_probe</span><span class="p">,</span>
<span class="p">};</span>
<span class="n">module_i2c_driver</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">my_hwmon_driver</span><span class="p">);</span>

<span class="n">MODULE_LICENSE</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s">"GPL"</span><span class="p">);</span>
<span class="n">MODULE_DESCRIPTION</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s">"Example out-of-tree hwmon driver for BMC"</span><span class="p">);</span>
```

</div></div>

### Yocto Recipe Using module.bbclass

    

```bitbake
# my-hwmon-module_1.0.bb
SUMMARY = "Out-of-tree hwmon driver for vendor sensor"
LICENSE = "GPL-2.0-only"
LIC_FILES_CHKSUM = "file://my_hwmon_driver.c;beginline=1;endline=1;md5=..."

SRC_URI = " \
    file://Makefile \
    file://my_hwmon_driver.c \
    file://my-hwmon-module.conf \
"

S = "${WORKDIR}"

inherit module

# Autoload at boot
KERNEL_MODULE_AUTOLOAD += "my_hwmon_driver"

# Install autoload config
do_install:append() {
    install -d ${D}${sysconfdir}/modules-load.d
    install -m 0644 ${WORKDIR}/my-hwmon-module.conf \
        ${D}${sysconfdir}/modules-load.d/
}
```

The `inherit module` line pulls in `module.bbclass`, which handles cross-compilation against the kernel headers, module signing (if enabled), and packaging into the correct `/lib/modules//` directory.

### Module Autoloading

    

Create a `.conf` file for `/etc/modules-load.d/`:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># files/my-hwmon-module.conf</span>
<span class="c"># Load vendor hwmon driver at boot</span>
my_hwmon_driver
```

</div></div>

Alternatively, use `KERNEL_MODULE_AUTOLOAD` in the recipe (shown above) which writes the appropriate config automatically.

### Building and Testing

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Build just the module recipe</span>
bitbake my-hwmon-module

<span class="c"># Build the full image (includes the module)</span>
bitbake obmc-phosphor-image

<span class="c"># On the running BMC, verify the module</span>
lsmod | <span class="nb">grep </span>my_hwmon
modinfo my_hwmon_driver
```

</div></div>
---

## Userspace Driver Alternatives

    

Not every hardware interaction requires a kernel driver. For simple register reads, GPIO toggling, or I2C device testing, userspace access is faster to develop and easier to debug. This section helps you decide when a userspace approach is sufficient.

### Decision Framework: Kernel Driver vs Userspace

    

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Criterion | Kernel Driver | Userspace Access |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Interrupt handling** | Required — only kernel can register IRQ handlers | Not possible (polling only) |
| **Latency requirements** | Microsecond-level response | Millisecond-level acceptable |
| **Shared device access** | Kernel manages arbitration | Single process at a time |
| **DMA support** | Full DMA engine access | Not available |
| **Upstream acceptance** | Required for OpenBMC mainline | Not applicable — stays in your layer |
| **Development speed** | Slower (compile, deploy, reboot) | Fast (edit, run) |
| **Debugging** | Kernel oops, printk, ftrace | gdb, printf, strace |
| **hwmon/D-Bus integration** | Automatic via hwmon subsystem | Manual — must write your own bridge |

</div>

If your device needs to appear as a standard hwmon sensor on D-Bus (for dbus-sensors/entity-manager integration), you almost always need a kernel driver. Userspace approaches are best for prototyping, diagnostics, and one-off access.

### libgpiod — GPIO Access

    

libgpiod v2 is the recommended way to access GPIO lines from userspace. It replaces the deprecated sysfs GPIO interface (`/sys/class/gpio/`).

**Command-line tools:**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># List all GPIO chips</span>
gpiodetect

<span class="c"># Show lines on a specific chip</span>
gpioinfo gpiochip0

<span class="c"># Read a GPIO line value</span>
gpioget gpiochip0 42

<span class="c"># Set a GPIO line (active-high)</span>
gpioset gpiochip0 <span class="nv">42</span><span class="o">=</span>1

<span class="c"># Monitor a line for events (rising/falling edge)</span>
gpiomon gpiochip0 42
```

</div></div>

**C API snippet:**

<div class="language-c highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="cp">#include</span> <span class="cpf"><gpiod.h></span><span class="cp">
</span>
<span class="k">struct</span> <span class="n">gpiod_chip</span> <span class="o">*</span><span class="n">chip</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">gpiod_chip_open</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s">"/dev/gpiochip0"</span><span class="p">);</span>
<span class="k">struct</span> <span class="n">gpiod_line_settings</span> <span class="o">*</span><span class="n">settings</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">gpiod_line_settings_new</span><span class="p">();</span>
<span class="n">gpiod_line_settings_set_direction</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">settings</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">GPIOD_LINE_DIRECTION_INPUT</span><span class="p">);</span>

<span class="k">struct</span> <span class="n">gpiod_line_config</span> <span class="o">*</span><span class="n">config</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">gpiod_line_config_new</span><span class="p">();</span>
<span class="k">static</span> <span class="k">const</span> <span class="kt">unsigned</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">offset</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">42</span><span class="p">;</span>
<span class="n">gpiod_line_config_add_line_settings</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">config</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="o">&</span><span class="n">offset</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">settings</span><span class="p">);</span>

<span class="k">struct</span> <span class="n">gpiod_line_request</span> <span class="o">*</span><span class="n">request</span> <span class="o">=</span>
    <span class="n">gpiod_chip_request_lines</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">chip</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nb">NULL</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">config</span><span class="p">);</span>

<span class="k">enum</span> <span class="n">gpiod_line_value</span> <span class="n">value</span> <span class="o">=</span>
    <span class="n">gpiod_line_request_get_value</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">request</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">offset</span><span class="p">);</span>

<span class="n">gpiod_line_request_release</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">request</span><span class="p">);</span>
<span class="n">gpiod_line_config_free</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">config</span><span class="p">);</span>
<span class="n">gpiod_line_settings_free</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">settings</span><span class="p">);</span>
<span class="n">gpiod_chip_close</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">chip</span><span class="p">);</span>
```

</div></div>

OpenBMC uses libgpiod extensively in `phosphor-gpio-monitor` and `phosphor-buttons`. See the [GPIO Management Guide](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/docs/03-core-services/14-gpio-management-guide.html) for the full OpenBMC GPIO architecture.

### i2c-dev / i2c-tools — Direct I2C Access

    

The `i2c-dev` kernel module exposes I2C buses as `/dev/i2c-N` character devices.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># List I2C buses</span>
i2cdetect <span class="nt">-l</span>

<span class="c"># Scan for devices on bus 0</span>
i2cdetect <span class="nt">-y</span> 0

<span class="c"># Read a register (bus 0, device 0x48, register 0x00)</span>
i2cget <span class="nt">-y</span> 0 0x48 0x00 w

<span class="c"># Write a register</span>
i2cset <span class="nt">-y</span> 0 0x48 0x01 0x60 w

<span class="c"># Dump all registers</span>
i2cdump <span class="nt">-y</span> 0 0x48
```

</div></div>

Using `i2c-tools` on a bus where a kernel driver is already bound can cause bus contention and unpredictable behavior. Use `i2cdetect` to check if addresses show `UU` (already claimed by a driver).

### spidev — SPI Userspace Access

    

The `spidev` driver exposes SPI devices as `/dev/spidevB.C` (bus B, chip-select C).

Device tree binding:

```dts
&spi1 {
    status = "okay";

    spidev@0 {
        compatible = "linux,spidev";
        reg = <0>;
        spi-max-frequency = <10000000>;
    };
};
```

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Test SPI communication (requires spi-tools package)</span>
spi-config <span class="nt">-d</span> /dev/spidev1.0 <span class="nt">-q</span>
spi-pipe <span class="nt">-d</span> /dev/spidev1.0 <span class="nt">-s</span> 1000000 < data.bin <span class="o">></span> response.bin
```

</div></div>

### UIO — Userspace I/O for Register-Mapped Devices

    

UIO maps device registers directly into userspace memory, allowing you to write a full driver without kernel code. Useful for FPGA registers or vendor-specific control blocks.

Device tree binding:

```dts
my-device@1e6e0000 {
    compatible = "generic-uio";
    reg = <0x1e6e0000 0x1000>;
};
```

Kernel config fragment:

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
CONFIG_UIO=y
CONFIG_UIO_PDRV_GENIRQ=y
```

</div></div>

Userspace access:

<div class="language-c highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="cp">#include</span> <span class="cpf"><sys/mman.h></span><span class="cp">
#include</span> <span class="cpf"><fcntl.h></span><span class="cp">
</span>
<span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">fd</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">open</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s">"/dev/uio0"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">O_RDWR</span><span class="p">);</span>
<span class="kt">void</span> <span class="o">*</span><span class="n">regs</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">mmap</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nb">NULL</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="mh">0x1000</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">PROT_READ</span> <span class="o">|</span> <span class="n">PROT_WRITE</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">MAP_SHARED</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">fd</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">);</span>

<span class="kt">uint32_t</span> <span class="n">val</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">((</span><span class="k">volatile</span> <span class="kt">uint32_t</span> <span class="o">*</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="n">regs</span><span class="p">)[</span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">];</span>  <span class="c1">// Read register 0x00</span>
<span class="p">((</span><span class="k">volatile</span> <span class="kt">uint32_t</span> <span class="o">*</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="n">regs</span><span class="p">)[</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">]</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mh">0xDEADBEEF</span><span class="p">;</span>    <span class="c1">// Write register 0x04</span>

<span class="n">munmap</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">regs</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="mh">0x1000</span><span class="p">);</span>
<span class="n">close</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">fd</span><span class="p">);</span>
```

</div></div>

### /dev/mem and devmem2 — Direct Physical Memory Access

    

For quick register checks during debugging, `devmem2` reads and writes physical addresses directly.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Read SCU register on AST2600 (Silicon Revision)</span>
devmem2 0x1e6e2004 w

<span class="c"># Write a register</span>
devmem2 0x1e6e2000 w 0x1688A8A8
```

</div></div>

`/dev/mem` access bypasses all kernel protections. A wrong write can corrupt memory, hang the SoC, or brick the BMC. Use only for debugging on development systems. Production firmware should disable `/dev/mem` access (`CONFIG_STRICT_DEVMEM=y`).

---

## Driver Debugging

    

Debugging kernel drivers on a BMC is constrained: limited flash storage rules out large trace buffers, there is typically no JTAG/kgdb access, and the BMC may be the only management interface to the system. These techniques work within those constraints.

### dynamic_debug — Runtime Debug Prints

    

The `dynamic_debug` facility lets you enable `dev_dbg()` and `pr_debug()` messages at runtime without rebuilding the kernel. This is the single most useful driver debugging tool on a BMC.

**Enable for a specific module:**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Enable all debug prints in the lm75 driver</span>
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"module lm75 +p"</span> <span class="o">></span> /sys/kernel/debug/dynamic_debug/control

<span class="c"># Enable for a specific file</span>
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"file drivers/hwmon/lm75.c +p"</span> <span class="o">></span> /sys/kernel/debug/dynamic_debug/control

<span class="c"># Enable for a specific function</span>
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"func lm75_probe +p"</span> <span class="o">></span> /sys/kernel/debug/dynamic_debug/control

<span class="c"># Include function name and line number in output</span>
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"module lm75 +pflm"</span> <span class="o">></span> /sys/kernel/debug/dynamic_debug/control
```

</div></div>

**Flags:** `p` = print, `f` = function name, `l` = line number, `m` = module name, `t` = thread ID

**View output:**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
dmesg <span class="nt">-w</span>  <span class="c"># Follow kernel log in real time</span>
```

</div></div>

**Kernel config required:**

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
CONFIG_DYNAMIC_DEBUG=y
```

</div></div>

To enable debug messages early in boot (before userspace is up), add `dyndbg="module lm75 +p"` to the kernel command line in U-Boot or the device tree `chosen` node.

### ftrace — Probe Sequence Tracing

    

Use `ftrace` with the `function_graph` tracer to visualize the call chain during driver probe — invaluable for understanding why a probe fails or hangs.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Enable function_graph tracer</span>
<span class="nb">echo </span>function_graph <span class="o">></span> /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/current_tracer

<span class="c"># Filter to your driver's functions</span>
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"lm75_*"</span> <span class="o">></span> /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/set_ftrace_filter

<span class="c"># Or trace the entire I2C subsystem</span>
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"i2c_*"</span> <span class="o">>></span> /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/set_ftrace_filter

<span class="c"># Start tracing</span>
<span class="nb">echo </span>1 <span class="o">></span> /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/tracing_on

<span class="c"># Trigger a probe (rebind the driver)</span>
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"0-0048"</span> <span class="o">></span> /sys/bus/i2c/drivers/lm75/unbind
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"0-0048"</span> <span class="o">></span> /sys/bus/i2c/drivers/lm75/bind

<span class="c"># Stop and read the trace</span>
<span class="nb">echo </span>0 <span class="o">></span> /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/tracing_on
<span class="nb">cat</span> /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/trace
```

</div></div>

**Example output:**

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
1)               |  lm75_probe() {
 1)   0.834 us    |    devm_regmap_init_i2c();
 1)   0.417 us    |    regmap_read();
 1)               |    devm_hwmon_device_register_with_info() {
 1)   1.250 us    |      hwmon_device_register_with_info();
 1)   1.667 us    |    }
 1)   4.584 us    |  }
```

</div></div>

On memory-constrained BMCs, reduce the trace buffer: `echo 512 > /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/buffer_size_kb` (default is often 1408 KB per CPU).

### debugfs Interfaces

    

Several kernel subsystems expose debugging information through debugfs:

**GPIO state:**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="nb">cat</span> /sys/kernel/debug/gpio
<span class="c"># Shows all registered GPIO chips, claimed lines, direction, and value</span>
```

</div></div>

**I2C bus information:**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># If CONFIG_I2C_DEBUG_CORE is enabled</span>
<span class="nb">ls</span> /sys/kernel/debug/i2c/
```

</div></div>

**Regmap register dumps:**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># If your driver uses regmap, its registers are exposed automatically</span>
<span class="nb">cat</span> /sys/kernel/debug/regmap/0-0048/registers
```

</div></div>

**Clock tree (useful for SoC debugging):**

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="nb">cat</span> /sys/kernel/debug/clk/clk_summary
```

</div></div>

### dmesg Patterns for Common Probe Failures

    

When a driver fails to probe, `dmesg` contains the clues. Here are the patterns to look for:

**Missing device tree node:**

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
# No output at all for your driver — it was never matched
# Check: does your DTS node have the right compatible string?
cat /proc/device-tree/soc/apb/bus@1e78a000/i2c-bus@100/temperature-sensor@48/compatible
```

</div></div>

**Wrong compatible string:**

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
# Driver loads but never probes — compatible mismatch
# Compare driver's of_match_table with DTS compatible
cat /sys/bus/i2c/drivers/lm75/module/drivers
```

</div></div>

**Deferred probe:**

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
lm75 0-0048: probe deferral - supplier not ready
# A dependency (regulator, clock, GPIO) isn't available yet
# Check: cat /sys/kernel/debug/devices_deferred
```

</div></div>

**I2C communication failure:**

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
lm75 0-0048: Failed to read register 0x00: -6
# -6 = ENXIO (no device at that address)
# Verify with: i2cdetect -y 0
```

</div></div>

**Missing kernel config:**

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
# modprobe: FATAL: Module lm75 not found
# Check: zcat /proc/config.gz | grep LM75
```

</div></div>
---

## I2C/SPI Sensor Binding Walkthrough

    

This end-to-end walkthrough traces the full path for adding an I2C hwmon sensor to an OpenBMC system, from device tree to Redfish visibility. We use the **TI TMP175** temperature sensor as the running example — it is supported by the `lm75` kernel driver and works in QEMU.

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌───────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────┐
│ Device   │───>│ Kernel   │───>│ hwmon    │───>│ Entity        │───>│ dbus-       │───>│ Redfish │
│ Tree     │    │ Driver   │    │ sysfs    │    │ Manager       │    │ sensors     │    │         │
│ Node     │    │ Binding  │    │ Interface│    │ JSON Config   │    │ D-Bus Expose│    │ Sensor  │
└──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └───────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────┘
```

</div></div>

### Step 1: Device Tree Node

    

Add the sensor to your platform’s device tree on the appropriate I2C bus:

```dts
&i2c0 {
    status = "okay";

    temperature-sensor@48 {
        compatible = "ti,tmp175";
        reg = <0x48>;
    };
};
```

Key fields:

* **`compatible`**: Must match a string in the kernel driver’s `of_device_id` table. For TMP175, the `lm75` driver matches `"ti,tmp175"`.
* **`reg`**: The 7-bit I2C address. TMP175 defaults to `0x48` (A0=A1=A2=GND).
* **Node name**: Convention is `@`, e.g., `temperature-sensor@48`.

### Step 2: Kernel Driver Binding

    

The kernel’s I2C subsystem matches the DTS `compatible` string against registered drivers. For TMP175:

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
Driver: drivers/hwmon/lm75.c
Compatible table entry: { .compatible = "ti,tmp175", .data = &tmp175 }
```

</div></div>

At boot, when the I2C bus is initialized, the kernel:

1. Parses the DTS node and creates an `i2c_client` for address `0x48`
2. Matches `"ti,tmp175"` to the `lm75` driver
3. Calls `lm75_probe()`, which reads chip ID registers and creates an hwmon device

Verify binding succeeded:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Check driver bound to device</span>
<span class="nb">ls</span> <span class="nt">-la</span> /sys/bus/i2c/devices/0-0048/driver
<span class="c"># Should show: ... -> ../../../bus/i2c/drivers/lm75</span>

<span class="c"># Check dmesg for probe</span>
dmesg | <span class="nb">grep </span>lm75
<span class="c"># lm75 0-0048: hwmon0: sensor 'tmp175'</span>
```

</div></div>

### Step 3: hwmon sysfs Verification

    

Once the driver probes successfully, it exposes temperature readings through the hwmon sysfs interface:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Find the hwmon device</span>
<span class="nb">ls</span> /sys/class/hwmon/
<span class="c"># hwmon0</span>

<span class="c"># Check which driver owns it</span>
<span class="nb">cat</span> /sys/class/hwmon/hwmon0/name
<span class="c"># tmp175</span>

<span class="c"># Read temperature (in millidegrees Celsius)</span>
<span class="nb">cat</span> /sys/class/hwmon/hwmon0/temp1_input
<span class="c"># 25000  (= 25.0°C)</span>

<span class="c"># Read all attributes</span>
<span class="nb">ls</span> /sys/class/hwmon/hwmon0/
<span class="c"># name  temp1_input  temp1_max  temp1_max_hyst  ...</span>
```

</div></div>

The `temp1_input` value is in millidegrees Celsius. Divide by 1000 for the human-readable temperature (25000 = 25.0°C).

### Step 4: Entity-Manager JSON Configuration

    

Entity-manager discovers hardware based on JSON configuration files. Create an entry for your platform that describes the sensor:

<div class="language-json highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"Exposes"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"Name"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"Baseboard Temp"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"Type"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"TMP175"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"Bus"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"Address"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"0x48"</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="p">],</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"Name"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"My Platform Baseboard"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"Probe"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"TRUE"</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
</span>
```

</div></div>

Place this JSON in your meta-layer’s entity-manager configurations directory:

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
meta-vendor/meta-platform/
  recipes-phosphor/configuration/
    entity-manager/
      my-platform-baseboard.json
```

</div></div>

See the [Entity Manager Guide](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/docs/03-core-services/03-entity-manager-guide.html) for advanced probe expressions and configuration patterns.

### Step 5: dbus-sensors Pickup and D-Bus Exposure

    

The `dbus-sensors` package includes `hwmontempsensor`, which monitors entity-manager for matching configurations and exposes hwmon readings on D-Bus.

Once entity-manager publishes the configuration, `hwmontempsensor` automatically:

1. Matches the `Type` field to its supported sensor types
2. Opens the corresponding `/sys/class/hwmon/` sysfs path
3. Creates a D-Bus object at `/xyz/openbmc_project/sensors/temperature/Baseboard_Temp`
4. Polls the sysfs value and updates the D-Bus property

Verify on D-Bus:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># List temperature sensors</span>
busctl tree xyz.openbmc_project.HwmonTempSensor

<span class="c"># Read the sensor value</span>
busctl get-property xyz.openbmc_project.HwmonTempSensor <span class="se">\</span>
    /xyz/openbmc_project/sensors/temperature/Baseboard_Temp <span class="se">\</span>
    xyz.openbmc_project.Sensor.Value Value
<span class="c"># d 25.0</span>
```

</div></div>

See the [D-Bus Sensors Guide](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/docs/03-core-services/01-dbus-sensors-guide.html) and [hwmon Sensors Guide](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/docs/03-core-services/02-hwmon-sensors-guide.html) for sensor types and thresholds.

### Step 6: Redfish Sensor Visibility

    

BMCWeb exposes D-Bus sensor objects as Redfish Sensor resources automatically:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Query chassis sensors</span>
curl <span class="nt">-k</span> <span class="nt">-u</span> root:0penBmc <span class="se">\</span>
    https://localhost:2443/redfish/v1/Chassis/chassis/Sensors/temperature_Baseboard_Temp
```

</div></div>

Expected response (excerpt):

<div class="language-json highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"@odata.id"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"/redfish/v1/Chassis/chassis/Sensors/temperature_Baseboard_Temp"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"Name"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"Baseboard Temp"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"Reading"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mf">25.0</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"ReadingUnits"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"Cel"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"ReadingType"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"Temperature"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"Status"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="nl">"State"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"Enabled"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="nl">"Health"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"OK"</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
</span>
```

</div></div>

## Upstreaming Best Practices

    

### OpenBMC Upstream-First Policy

    

The OpenBMC kernel tree’s development policy is **“code must be upstream first.”** Code enters the OpenBMC kernel in order of preference:

1. **Upstream release integration** — arrives automatically when OpenBMC advances kernel versions
2. **Backporting** — cherry-picking accepted upstream commits to the current OpenBMC branch
3. **Temporary carry patches** — held in the OpenBMC tree while upstream review is ongoing (least preferred)

### Commit Message Format

    

Follow the Linux kernel commit message conventions:

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
subsystem: component: Short description (under 50 chars)

Detailed explanation of the change. Explain the problem being solved
and why this approach was chosen. Wrap at 72 characters.

Tested on ast2600-evb QEMU and physical hardware.

Signed-off-by: Your Name <your.email@example.com>
```

</div></div>

### Submission to Upstream Linux

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Format patches for upstream</span>
git format-patch <span class="nt">-1</span> <span class="nt">--cc</span><span class="o">=</span>openbmc@lists.ozlabs.org

<span class="c"># Send via email to the subsystem maintainer</span>
git send-email <span class="nt">--to</span><span class="o">=</span>maintainer@kernel.org <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--cc</span><span class="o">=</span>openbmc@lists.ozlabs.org <span class="se">\</span>
  0001-my-patch.patch
```

</div></div>

### Submission to OpenBMC Kernel Tree

    

For patches carried temporarily in the OpenBMC tree:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
git format-patch <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--subject-prefix</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s2">"PATCH linux dev-6.18"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--to</span><span class="o">=</span>openbmc@lists.ozlabs.org <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-1</span>
```

</div></div>

Push to Gerrit for code review:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
git push gerrit HEAD:refs/for/dev-6.18
```

</div></div>

## Troubleshooting

    

### Issue: Patch Fails to Apply

    

**Symptom**: BitBake errors with “Patch failed” during `do_patch`

**Cause**: The patch was generated against a different kernel version or conflicts with other patches in the layer stack.

**Solution**:

1. Check the base commit your patch was generated from
2. Use `devtool modify linux-aspeed` to get the exact source BitBake uses
3. Regenerate the patch against that source:
    
```
cd build/workspace/sources/linux-aspeed
# Apply your changes, commit, then:
git format-patch -1
```

### Issue: Config Option Not Taking Effect

    

**Symptom**: Your `.cfg` fragment sets `CONFIG_MY_OPTION=y` but the final `.config` has it unset

**Cause**: A dependency is missing, or another config overrides yours.

**Solution**:

1. Run `bitbake linux-aspeed -c kernel_configcheck -f` to see warnings
2. Check dependencies in `menuconfig` — the option may require a parent option
3. Add the parent option to your fragment as well

### Issue: devtool modify Uses Wrong defconfig

    

**Symptom**: After `devtool modify`, the kernel builds with an incorrect or minimal config

**Cause**: Known issue ([openbmc/openbmc#3294](https://github.com/openbmc/openbmc/issues/3294)) where devtool may not apply machine-specific defconfig correctly.

**Solution**:

1. Manually copy the correct defconfig:
    
```
cp meta-aspeed/recipes-kernel/linux/linux-aspeed/aspeed-g6/defconfig \
  build/workspace/sources/linux-aspeed/.config
```
2. Or use the bbappend workflow instead of devtool for the final integration

### Issue: Kernel Boots But Driver Not Found

    

**Symptom**: `modprobe my_driver` returns “Module not found” or device is not detected at boot

**Cause**: Driver not enabled in kernel config, or device tree node missing/incorrect.

**Solution**:

1. Verify config: `zcat /proc/config.gz | grep MY_DRIVER`
2. Verify DTS node: `ls /proc/device-tree/soc/...`
3. Check `dmesg` for probe failures: `dmesg | grep -i error`

## Quick Reference

    

### Essential Commands

    

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Check out kernel for editing | `devtool modify linux-aspeed` |
| Build kernel only | `devtool build linux-aspeed` |
| Interactive config editor | `bitbake linux-aspeed -c menuconfig` |
| Generate config diff | `bitbake linux-aspeed -c diffconfig` |
| Validate config fragments | `bitbake linux-aspeed -c kernel_configcheck -f` |
| Save current config as defconfig | `bitbake linux-aspeed -c savedefconfig` |
| Export patches to layer | `devtool finish linux-aspeed ~/meta-mylayer` |
| Clean up workspace | `devtool reset linux-aspeed` |
| Force re-patch | `bitbake linux-aspeed -c patch -f` |
| Full rebuild from scratch | `bitbake linux-aspeed -c cleansstate && bitbake linux-aspeed` |
| Build out-of-tree module | `bitbake my-hwmon-module` |
| Enable dynamic debug for module | `echo "module lm75 +p" > /sys/kernel/debug/dynamic_debug/control` |
| Start ftrace function_graph | `echo function_graph > /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/current_tracer` |
| Check GPIO state via debugfs | `cat /sys/kernel/debug/gpio` |
| Scan I2C bus | `i2cdetect -y 0` |
| Read I2C register | `i2cget -y 0 0x48 0x00 w` |
| Check deferred probes | `cat /sys/kernel/debug/devices_deferred` |

</div>
