## Overview

    

Secure boot ensures that every piece of firmware executed on the BMC is cryptographically verified before it runs. On ASPEED AST2600 platforms, the secure boot chain begins at the hardware level with a Root of Trust stored in One-Time Programmable (OTP) fuses and extends through each boot stage up to the Linux kernel.

This guide walks you through the complete secure boot lifecycle: understanding the chain of trust, generating and provisioning cryptographic keys, integrating image signing into the Yocto build, and managing keys across development and production environments. You will learn how each boot stage verifies the next, how the ASPEED `socsec` tool signs firmware images, and how OTP fuse programming permanently binds a platform to a specific Root of Trust.

Secure boot is essential for production BMC deployments where firmware integrity must be guaranteed. Without it, an attacker with flash access can replace BMC firmware with a malicious image. With secure boot enabled, the hardware rejects any firmware that does not carry a valid signature from the provisioned Root of Trust key.

**Key concepts covered:**

* AST2600 secure boot chain of trust (OTP through kernel)
* RSA key pair generation and OTP fuse provisioning
* ASPEED `socsec` tool for image signing
* Yocto build integration for automated signing
* Development vs production key management
* Security strap configuration and jumper handling

**OTP programming is irreversible.** Once you burn a public key hash into OTP fuses, you cannot change or revoke it. A mistake during OTP provisioning can permanently brick the platform. Always verify your key material and OTP configuration on development boards before touching production hardware.

**Requires real hardware.** While you can test the signing workflow and build signed images using QEMU, OTP programming and actual secure boot verification require a physical AST2600 board. QEMU does not emulate OTP fuses or the ROM-based signature verification.

---

## Architecture

    

### AST2600 Secure Boot Chain

    

The AST2600 implements a multi-stage verified boot process. Each stage verifies the cryptographic signature of the next stage before transferring control. If any verification fails, the boot process halts.

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  AST2600 Secure Boot Chain                      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  ┌──────────────────┐                                           │
│  │   ASPEED ROM     │  Immutable code in silicon                │
│  │   (Boot ROM)     │  Reads OTP Root of Trust public key hash  │
│  └────────┬─────────┘                                           │
│           │  Verifies RSA signature                             │
│           ▼                                                     │
│  ┌──────────────────┐                                           │
│  │   U-Boot SPL     │  First mutable firmware stage             │
│  │   (Secondary     │  Signed with private key matching OTP     │
│  │    Program       │  ROM compares signature against OTP hash  │
│  │    Loader)       │                                           │
│  └────────┬─────────┘                                           │
│           │  Verifies RSA signature                             │
│           ▼                                                     │
│  ┌──────────────────┐                                           │
│  │   U-Boot         │  Full bootloader                          │
│  │   (Proper)       │  SPL verifies signature before loading    │
│  │                  │  Initializes DRAM, loads FIT image        │
│  └────────┬─────────┘                                           │
│           │  Verifies FIT image signature                       │
│           ▼                                                     │
│  ┌──────────────────┐                                           │
│  │   Linux Kernel   │  Kernel + DTB in signed FIT image         │
│  │   (FIT Image)    │  U-Boot verifies before booting           │
│  │                  │  Includes initramfs if configured         │
│  └──────────────────┘                                           │
│                                                                 │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  OTP Fuses (Root of Trust)                               │   │
│  │  ── RSA public key hash (SHA-256/SHA-512)                │   │
│  │  ── Security strap bits (enable/disable secure boot)     │   │
│  │  ── Key revocation bits (for key rotation)               │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

</div></div>

### Verification Flow Summary

    

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Boot Stage | Verified By | Signature Type | Key Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| U-Boot SPL | ASPEED Boot ROM | RSA-2048/4096 + SHA-256 | OTP fuse (public key hash) |
| U-Boot | U-Boot SPL | RSA-2048/4096 + SHA-256 | Embedded in SPL image |
| Linux Kernel (FIT) | U-Boot | RSA-2048/4096 + SHA-256 | Embedded in U-Boot DTB |

</div>

### Key Dependencies

    

* **ASPEED Boot ROM**: The immutable first-stage bootloader in silicon. It reads OTP fuses to determine whether secure boot is enabled and which public key hash to use for verification.
* **socsec**: ASPEED’s command-line tool for signing images, generating OTP configuration, and programming fuses. Part of the `socsec` Python package.
* **OpenSSL**: Used for RSA key pair generation. The private key signs images; the public key hash is burned into OTP.
* **U-Boot FIT signing**: U-Boot’s Flattened Image Tree (FIT) format supports embedded RSA signatures for kernel and DTB verification.

---

## OTP Key Provisioning

    

OTP (One-Time Programmable) fuses provide the hardware Root of Trust for the secure boot chain. You program the SHA-256 hash of your RSA public key into the OTP region. The Boot ROM reads this hash at every boot to verify the SPL signature.

### Step 1: Generate an RSA Key Pair

    

Generate a 4096-bit RSA key pair using OpenSSL. This key pair is the foundation of your entire secure boot chain.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Create a directory for your secure boot keys</span>
<span class="nb">mkdir</span> <span class="nt">-p</span> ~/secure-boot-keys <span class="o">&&</span> <span class="nb">cd</span> ~/secure-boot-keys

<span class="c"># Generate 4096-bit RSA private key</span>
openssl genrsa <span class="nt">-out</span> rsa4096_private.pem 4096

<span class="c"># Extract the public key</span>
openssl rsa <span class="nt">-in</span> rsa4096_private.pem <span class="nt">-pubout</span> <span class="nt">-out</span> rsa4096_public.pem

<span class="c"># Verify the key pair</span>
openssl rsa <span class="nt">-in</span> rsa4096_private.pem <span class="nt">-check</span> <span class="nt">-noout</span>
```

</div></div>

Use RSA-4096 for production deployments. RSA-2048 is acceptable for development and testing but provides a smaller security margin for long-lived platforms.

For development boards, you may choose RSA-2048 for faster signing and verification:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Development-only: 2048-bit key (faster, lower security margin)</span>
openssl genrsa <span class="nt">-out</span> rsa2048_dev_private.pem 2048
openssl rsa <span class="nt">-in</span> rsa2048_dev_private.pem <span class="nt">-pubout</span> <span class="nt">-out</span> rsa2048_dev_public.pem
```

</div></div>

### Step 2: Install the socsec Tool

    

The ASPEED `socsec` tool handles OTP image generation, image signing, and OTP programming. Install it from PyPI or the ASPEED SDK.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Install socsec from PyPI</span>
pip3 <span class="nb">install </span>socsec

<span class="c"># Verify installation</span>
socsec <span class="nt">--version</span>

<span class="c"># Alternatively, clone from ASPEED's repository</span>
git clone https://github.com/AspeedTech-BMC/socsec.git
<span class="nb">cd </span>socsec <span class="o">&&</span> pip3 <span class="nb">install</span> <span class="nb">.</span>
```

</div></div>

### Step 3: Create the OTP Configuration

    

The OTP configuration file defines which fuse bits to program, including the public key hash and security strap settings. Create a JSON configuration for your platform.

<div class="language-json highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"version"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"A3"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"soc"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"2600"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"otp_info"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="nl">"conf"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"secure_boot_enable"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kc">true</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"secure_boot_header_offset"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"0x20"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"rsa_key_order"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"big_endian"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"sha_algorithm"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"SHA256"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"retire_key_id"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="p">},</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="nl">"strap"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"secure_boot"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kc">true</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"boot_from_emmc"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kc">false</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"enable_watchdog"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kc">true</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"uart_debug_disable"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kc">false</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="p">},</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="nl">"key"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"key_type"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"RSA4096_SHA256"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"number_of_keys"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"keys"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[</span><span class="w">
                </span><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
                    </span><span class="nl">"key_file"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"rsa4096_public.pem"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
                    </span><span class="nl">"key_id"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="w">
                </span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="p">]</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
</span>
```

</div></div>

Save this file as `otp_config.json` in your secure boot keys directory.

The `version` field must match your AST2600 silicon revision (A1, A3, etc.). Check your chip marking or datasheet. Using the wrong version causes OTP programming to fail or produce incorrect fuse values.

### Step 4: Generate the OTP Image

    

Use `socsec` to generate the OTP image from your configuration. This produces a binary that contains the fuse values to program.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Generate OTP image</span>
socsec make_otp_image <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--config</span> otp_config.json <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--output</span> otp_image.bin

<span class="c"># Verify the generated OTP image contents</span>
socsec verify_otp_image <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--config</span> otp_config.json <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--image</span> otp_image.bin
```

</div></div>

The tool reads your public key, computes its SHA-256 hash, and embeds it in the OTP image along with the strap and configuration bits.

### Step 5: Program OTP Fuses

    

**This step is irreversible.** Once OTP fuses are programmed, they cannot be erased or modified. Double-check your configuration and key material before proceeding. Perform this step on a development board first.

Program the OTP fuses using `socsec` over the ASPEED debug UART or JTAG interface:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Connect to the AST2600 via debug UART</span>
<span class="c"># Ensure the board is in OTP programming mode (security jumper set)</span>

<span class="c"># Program OTP fuses</span>
socsec otp_prog <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--image</span> otp_image.bin <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--port</span> /dev/ttyUSB0 <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--baud</span> 115200

<span class="c"># Read back and verify OTP contents</span>
socsec otp_read <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--port</span> /dev/ttyUSB0 <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--baud</span> 115200 <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--output</span> otp_readback.bin
```

</div></div>

After programming, compare the readback with your expected values:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Diff the programmed values against expected</span>
socsec otp_verify <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--config</span> otp_config.json <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--image</span> otp_readback.bin
```

</div></div>

### Security Strap Configuration

    

The AST2600 has hardware strap pins that interact with OTP security settings. These straps control boot behavior during development.

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Strap Pin | Function | Development | Production |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `SCU510[1]` | Secure boot enable | 0 (disabled) | 1 (enabled via OTP) |
| `SCU510[2]` | Boot source select | SPI (default) | SPI |
| `SCU510[4]` | UART debug | Enabled | Disabled |
| `SCU510[6]` | JTAG debug | Enabled | Disabled |

</div>

During development, keep UART and JTAG debug enabled in the strap configuration. Disable them only in production OTP images. If you disable debug interfaces in OTP and your signed image fails to boot, you lose all debug access to the board.

---

## Image Signing Workflow

    

Once OTP fuses are provisioned with your public key hash, every firmware image must be signed with the corresponding private key. The ASPEED `socsec` tool signs U-Boot SPL and U-Boot images, while U-Boot itself handles FIT image (kernel) signing.

### Signing U-Boot SPL

    

The Boot ROM expects the SPL image to contain a signature header. Use `socsec` to wrap the SPL binary with a verified boot header.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Sign the U-Boot SPL binary</span>
socsec sign <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--image</span> u-boot-spl.bin <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--key</span> rsa4096_private.pem <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--algorithm</span> RSA4096_SHA256 <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--soc</span> 2600 <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--output</span> u-boot-spl-signed.bin

<span class="c"># Verify the signature offline (before flashing)</span>
socsec verify <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--image</span> u-boot-spl-signed.bin <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--key</span> rsa4096_public.pem <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--soc</span> 2600
```

</div></div>

The signed SPL binary includes:

* A signature header with the RSA signature
* The original SPL code
* Padding to align with the Boot ROM’s expectations

### Signing U-Boot Proper

    

U-Boot SPL verifies U-Boot proper using the same key infrastructure. Sign the U-Boot binary similarly:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Sign U-Boot proper</span>
socsec sign <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--image</span> u-boot.bin <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--key</span> rsa4096_private.pem <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--algorithm</span> RSA4096_SHA256 <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--soc</span> 2600 <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--output</span> u-boot-signed.bin

<span class="c"># Verify offline</span>
socsec verify <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--image</span> u-boot-signed.bin <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--key</span> rsa4096_public.pem <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--soc</span> 2600
```

</div></div>

### Signing the Kernel FIT Image

    

The Linux kernel, device tree, and optional initramfs are packaged into a FIT (Flattened Image Tree) image. U-Boot verifies the FIT image signature before booting.

FIT signing uses U-Boot’s built-in mechanism with `mkimage`:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Create a FIT image description (ITS file)</span>
<span class="c"># The ITS file references the kernel, DTB, and signing key</span>

<span class="c"># Sign the FIT image with mkimage</span>
mkimage <span class="nt">-f</span> fit-image.its <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-K</span> u-boot.dtb <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-k</span> ~/secure-boot-keys <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-r</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    fitImage

<span class="c"># The -K flag writes the public key into the U-Boot DTB</span>
<span class="c"># The -k flag specifies the directory containing the private key</span>
<span class="c"># The -r flag marks the key as "required" for verification</span>
```

</div></div>

The U-Boot DTB now contains the public key node. When U-Boot boots, it reads this key from its own DTB and uses it to verify the FIT image signature before launching the kernel.

### Verifying Signatures Offline

    

Always verify your signed images before flashing them to hardware:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Verify SPL signature</span>
socsec verify <span class="nt">--image</span> u-boot-spl-signed.bin <span class="nt">--key</span> rsa4096_public.pem <span class="nt">--soc</span> 2600
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"SPL verification: </span><span class="nv">$?</span><span class="s2">"</span>

<span class="c"># Verify U-Boot signature</span>
socsec verify <span class="nt">--image</span> u-boot-signed.bin <span class="nt">--key</span> rsa4096_public.pem <span class="nt">--soc</span> 2600
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"U-Boot verification: </span><span class="nv">$?</span><span class="s2">"</span>

<span class="c"># Verify FIT image signature using fit_check_sign (from U-Boot tools)</span>
fit_check_sign <span class="nt">-f</span> fitImage <span class="nt">-k</span> u-boot.dtb
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"FIT verification: </span><span class="nv">$?</span><span class="s2">"</span>
```

</div></div>

Add offline verification as a CI/CD step. Reject any build that produces images failing signature verification. This catches signing key mismatches and corrupted images before they reach hardware.

---

## Build-Time Signing Integration

    

The OpenBMC Yocto build system integrates secure boot signing into the image build process. You configure signing parameters in your machine configuration, and the build automatically signs all boot-stage images.

### Yocto Configuration

    

Add the following variables to your machine’s `local.conf` or `machine.conf`:

```bitbake
# Enable secure boot signing
SOCSEC_SIGN_ENABLE = "1"

# Path to the signing private key
SOCSEC_SIGN_KEY = "/path/to/secure-boot-keys/rsa4096_private.pem"

# Signing algorithm
SOCSEC_SIGN_ALGO = "RSA4096_SHA256"

# SOC type
SOCSEC_SIGN_SOC = "2600"

# Enable FIT image signing for the kernel
UBOOT_SIGN_ENABLE = "1"
UBOOT_SIGN_KEYNAME = "rsa4096"
UBOOT_SIGN_KEYDIR = "/path/to/secure-boot-keys"
UBOOT_MKIMAGE_DTCOPTS = "-I dts -O dtb -p 2000"
UBOOT_SIGN_IMG_KEYNAME = "rsa4096"
FIT_SIGN_INDIVIDUAL = "1"
```

### Recipe Integration

    

The `u-boot-aspeed-sdk` recipe (or your machine’s U-Boot recipe) picks up the signing configuration and invokes `socsec` during the build. The typical integration looks like this in the recipe’s bbappend:

```bitbake
# meta-<your-machine>/recipes-bsp/u-boot/u-boot-aspeed-sdk_%.bbappend

DEPENDS += "socsec-native"

do_deploy:append() {
    if [ "${SOCSEC_SIGN_ENABLE}" = "1" ]; then
        # Sign U-Boot SPL
        socsec sign \
            --image ${DEPLOYDIR}/u-boot-spl.bin \
            --key ${SOCSEC_SIGN_KEY} \
            --algorithm ${SOCSEC_SIGN_ALGO} \
            --soc ${SOCSEC_SIGN_SOC} \
            --output ${DEPLOYDIR}/u-boot-spl-signed.bin

        # Sign U-Boot proper
        socsec sign \
            --image ${DEPLOYDIR}/u-boot.bin \
            --key ${SOCSEC_SIGN_KEY} \
            --algorithm ${SOCSEC_SIGN_ALGO} \
            --soc ${SOCSEC_SIGN_SOC} \
            --output ${DEPLOYDIR}/u-boot-signed.bin

        # Replace unsigned images with signed versions
        install -m 0644 ${DEPLOYDIR}/u-boot-spl-signed.bin \
            ${DEPLOYDIR}/u-boot-spl.bin
        install -m 0644 ${DEPLOYDIR}/u-boot-signed.bin \
            ${DEPLOYDIR}/u-boot.bin
    fi
}
```

### Kernel FIT Signing in the Build

    

The kernel recipe uses U-Boot’s `mkimage` to sign the FIT image during the build. Enable this in your kernel bbappend:

```bitbake
# meta-<your-machine>/recipes-kernel/linux/linux-aspeed_%.bbappend

inherit kernel-fitimage

# These variables drive FIT signing
UBOOT_SIGN_ENABLE = "1"
UBOOT_SIGN_KEYNAME = "rsa4096"
UBOOT_SIGN_KEYDIR = "/path/to/secure-boot-keys"

# Include both kernel and DTB in the signed FIT
FIT_SIGN_INDIVIDUAL = "1"
KERNEL_CLASSES = "kernel-fitimage"
KERNEL_IMAGETYPE = "fitImage"
```

### Build and Verify

    

Run the full build and verify the output images carry valid signatures:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Build the image with signing enabled</span>
<span class="nb">cd </span>openbmc
<span class="nb">.</span> setup <your-machine>
bitbake obmc-phosphor-image

<span class="c"># Check the deploy directory for signed images</span>
<span class="nb">ls</span> <span class="nt">-la</span> build/tmp/deploy/images/<your-machine>/u-boot-spl.bin
<span class="nb">ls</span> <span class="nt">-la</span> build/tmp/deploy/images/<your-machine>/u-boot.bin
<span class="nb">ls</span> <span class="nt">-la</span> build/tmp/deploy/images/<your-machine>/fitImage

<span class="c"># Verify signatures offline</span>
socsec verify <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--image</span> build/tmp/deploy/images/<your-machine>/u-boot-spl.bin <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--key</span> ~/secure-boot-keys/rsa4096_public.pem <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--soc</span> 2600
```

</div></div>

The build system does not program OTP fuses. OTP provisioning is always a separate, explicit step performed directly on hardware. The build only produces signed images that are compatible with the OTP-provisioned key.

---

## Development vs Production Key Management

    

Managing cryptographic keys is the most critical aspect of secure boot operations. A compromised private key allows an attacker to sign malicious firmware that the hardware accepts as legitimate. The irreversible nature of OTP programming amplifies the stakes: once a public key hash is fused, the platform trusts that key permanently (unless key rotation slots are available).

### Key Hierarchy

    

Maintain separate key sets for development and production with clearly defined boundaries:

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Key Hierarchy                            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                             │
│  Development Keys                                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  Storage: Developer workstation or shared vault     │    │
│  │  Access:  All firmware developers                   │    │
│  │  OTP:     Burned only on development boards         │    │
│  │  Purpose: Prototyping, testing, CI builds           │    │
│  │  Type:    RSA-2048 or RSA-4096                      │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                             │
│  Production Keys                                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  Storage: Hardware Security Module (HSM)            │    │
│  │  Access:  Signing service only (no human access)    │    │
│  │  OTP:     Burned on production platforms            │    │
│  │  Purpose: Release builds, customer-facing firmware  │    │
│  │  Type:    RSA-4096 (minimum)                        │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                             │
│  Key Rotation Slots (OTP supports multiple key IDs)         │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  Slot 0: Primary production key (active)            │    │
│  │  Slot 1: Backup production key (provisioned, unused)│    │
│  │  Slot 2: Reserved for future rotation               │    │
│  │  Slot 3: Reserved                                   │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

</div></div>

### Development Key Practices

    

Use development keys for all prototyping and CI/CD workflows. These keys are known and shared among the team.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Generate a clearly labeled development key pair</span>
openssl genrsa <span class="nt">-out</span> dev_rsa4096_private.pem 4096
openssl rsa <span class="nt">-in</span> dev_rsa4096_private.pem <span class="nt">-pubout</span> <span class="nt">-out</span> dev_rsa4096_public.pem

<span class="c"># Store in version control (development keys ONLY)</span>
<span class="c"># NEVER store production keys in version control</span>
<span class="nb">cp </span>dev_rsa4096_private.pem ~/openbmc/meta-mymachine/conf/keys/
<span class="nb">cp </span>dev_rsa4096_public.pem ~/openbmc/meta-mymachine/conf/keys/
```

</div></div>

**Never reuse development keys for production.** Development keys stored in version control or on developer workstations are considered compromised by definition. Production hardware must use keys generated and stored exclusively in an HSM.

### Production Key Practices

    

Production keys must never leave the HSM. Use a signing service that accepts unsigned images and returns signed images without exposing the private key.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Production signing workflow (conceptual)</span>
<span class="c"># The private key never leaves the HSM</span>

<span class="c"># 1. Build unsigned images</span>
bitbake obmc-phosphor-image   <span class="c"># with SOCSEC_SIGN_ENABLE = "0"</span>

<span class="c"># 2. Submit unsigned images to the signing service</span>
curl <span class="nt">-X</span> POST https://signing-service.internal/sign <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-F</span> <span class="s2">"image=@u-boot-spl.bin"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-F</span> <span class="s2">"algorithm=RSA4096_SHA256"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-F</span> <span class="s2">"key_id=production_slot0"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-o</span> u-boot-spl-signed.bin

<span class="c"># 3. Verify the signature using the public key</span>
socsec verify <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--image</span> u-boot-spl-signed.bin <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--key</span> production_rsa4096_public.pem <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--soc</span> 2600
```

</div></div>

### OTP Key Rotation

    

The AST2600 OTP supports multiple key slots, allowing you to rotate keys without replacing hardware. However, key rotation is constrained by the number of available OTP slots (typically 4).

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Operation | Possible? | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add a new key to an empty slot | Yes | Program the new key hash into the next available slot |
| Retire an old key | Yes | Set the retire bit for the old key’s slot ID |
| Modify an existing key | No | OTP fuses are write-once; bits can be set but not cleared |
| Erase all keys | No | OTP is permanently programmed |
| Add keys beyond slot limit | No | Once all slots are used, no more keys can be added |

</div>

To rotate to a new key:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># 1. Generate a new key pair</span>
openssl genrsa <span class="nt">-out</span> rsa4096_rotation1_private.pem 4096
openssl rsa <span class="nt">-in</span> rsa4096_rotation1_private.pem <span class="nt">-pubout</span> <span class="nt">-out</span> rsa4096_rotation1_public.pem

<span class="c"># 2. Update OTP config to add the new key at slot 1 and retire slot 0</span>
<span class="c"># In otp_config.json:</span>
<span class="c">#   "retire_key_id": 0,</span>
<span class="c">#   "keys": [</span>
<span class="c">#     { "key_file": "rsa4096_public.pem", "key_id": 0 },</span>
<span class="c">#     { "key_file": "rsa4096_rotation1_public.pem", "key_id": 1 }</span>
<span class="c">#   ]</span>

<span class="c"># 3. Generate and program the updated OTP image</span>
socsec make_otp_image <span class="nt">--config</span> otp_config_rotation.json <span class="nt">--output</span> otp_rotation.bin
socsec otp_prog <span class="nt">--image</span> otp_rotation.bin <span class="nt">--port</span> /dev/ttyUSB0 <span class="nt">--baud</span> 115200

<span class="c"># 4. Sign all new images with the rotation key</span>
socsec sign <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--image</span> u-boot-spl.bin <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--key</span> rsa4096_rotation1_private.pem <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--algorithm</span> RSA4096_SHA256 <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--soc</span> 2600 <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--key-id</span> 1 <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--output</span> u-boot-spl-signed.bin
```

</div></div>

Plan your key rotation strategy before the initial OTP provisioning. Decide how many slots to reserve for rotation and document the key lifecycle for your platform.

---

## Security Jumper Handling

    

During development, you need the ability to disable secure boot for debugging and reflashing unsigned images. The AST2600 supports a hardware security jumper that overrides OTP strap settings.

### Jumper Configuration

    

Most AST2600 evaluation boards provide a jumper header for secure boot override:

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Jumper State | Boot Behavior | Use Case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open (default) | OTP straps control boot | Production / secure boot active |
| Closed | Secure boot bypassed | Development / recovery |

</div>

When the security jumper is closed:

* The Boot ROM skips SPL signature verification
* Unsigned images boot normally
* UART and JTAG debug remain available regardless of OTP settings
* OTP fuse contents are not modified (the jumper only bypasses enforcement)

Label development boards clearly with their jumper state and OTP provisioning status. A board with OTP fuses programmed but the security jumper closed looks identical to an unprovisioned board during boot, which can cause confusion during testing.

### Recovery Procedure

    

If a board with secure boot enabled fails to boot a signed image (for example, due to a corrupted flash), use the security jumper to recover:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># 1. Power off the board</span>
<span class="c"># 2. Close the security jumper (bypass secure boot)</span>
<span class="c"># 3. Power on — board boots unsigned recovery image or enters UART recovery mode</span>
<span class="c"># 4. Reflash a correctly signed image via UART or SPI programmer</span>

<span class="c"># UART recovery using ASPEED's uart_flash tool</span>
socsec uart_flash <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--port</span> /dev/ttyUSB0 <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--baud</span> 115200 <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">--image</span> flash-<machine>.bin

<span class="c"># 5. Power off</span>
<span class="c"># 6. Open the security jumper (re-enable secure boot)</span>
<span class="c"># 7. Power on — board boots the newly flashed signed image</span>
```

</div></div>

The security jumper must be removed (open) on production systems. A closed security jumper completely defeats the purpose of secure boot. Include jumper state verification in your manufacturing and deployment checklists.

---

## Code Examples

    

### Example 1: Key Generation Script

    

A complete script for generating development key pairs and OTP configuration:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c">#!/bin/bash</span>
<span class="c"># generate-dev-keys.sh</span>
<span class="c"># Generate development secure boot keys for AST2600</span>

<span class="nb">set</span> <span class="nt">-euo</span> pipefail

<span class="nv">KEY_DIR</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">1</span><span class="k">:-</span><span class="p">./dev-keys</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">"</span>
<span class="nv">KEY_SIZE</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">2</span><span class="k">:-</span><span class="nv">4096</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">"</span>
<span class="nv">SOC_VERSION</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">3</span><span class="k">:-</span><span class="nv">A3</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">"</span>

<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"Generating </span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">KEY_SIZE</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">-bit RSA development keys in </span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">KEY_DIR</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">..."</span>

<span class="nb">mkdir</span> <span class="nt">-p</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">KEY_DIR</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">"</span>

<span class="c"># Generate RSA private key</span>
openssl genrsa <span class="nt">-out</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">KEY_DIR</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">/dev_rsa</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">KEY_SIZE</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">_private.pem"</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">KEY_SIZE</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">"</span>

<span class="c"># Extract public key</span>
openssl rsa <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-in</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">KEY_DIR</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">/dev_rsa</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">KEY_SIZE</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">_private.pem"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-pubout</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-out</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">KEY_DIR</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">/dev_rsa</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">KEY_SIZE</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">_public.pem"</span>

<span class="c"># Display key fingerprint for verification</span>
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"Public key fingerprint:"</span>
openssl rsa <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-pubin</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-in</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">KEY_DIR</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">/dev_rsa</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">KEY_SIZE</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">_public.pem"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-outform</span> DER 2>/dev/null | <span class="nb">sha256sum</span>

<span class="c"># Generate OTP configuration</span>
<span class="nb">cat</span> <span class="o">></span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">KEY_DIR</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">/otp_config_dev.json"</span> <span class="o"><<</span> <span class="no">OTPEOF</span><span class="sh">
{
    "version": "</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">SOC_VERSION</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="sh">",
    "soc": "2600",
    "otp_info": {
        "conf": {
            "secure_boot_enable": true,
            "secure_boot_header_offset": "0x20",
            "rsa_key_order": "big_endian",
            "sha_algorithm": "SHA256",
            "retire_key_id": 0
        },
        "strap": {
            "secure_boot": true,
            "boot_from_emmc": false,
            "enable_watchdog": true,
            "uart_debug_disable": false
        },
        "key": {
            "key_type": "RSA</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">KEY_SIZE</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="sh">_SHA256",
            "number_of_keys": 1,
            "keys": [
                {
                    "key_file": "dev_rsa</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">KEY_SIZE</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="sh">_public.pem",
                    "key_id": 0
                }
            ]
        }
    }
}
</span><span class="no">OTPEOF

</span><span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"Development keys and OTP config generated in </span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">KEY_DIR</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">/"</span>
<span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"WARNING: These are DEVELOPMENT keys. Never use them for production."</span>
```

</div></div>

See the complete example at [examples/secure-boot/](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/docs/examples/secure-boot/README.md).

### Example 2: Build-Time Signing Verification Script

    

A script to verify all signed images after a build completes:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c">#!/bin/bash</span>
<span class="c"># verify-signed-images.sh</span>
<span class="c"># Verify all secure boot signatures after an OpenBMC build</span>

<span class="nb">set</span> <span class="nt">-euo</span> pipefail

<span class="nv">DEPLOY_DIR</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">1</span>:?Usage:<span class="p"> </span><span class="nv">$0</span><span class="p"> <deploy-dir> 
}"
PUBLIC_KEY="${2:?Usage: $0  }"
SOC="2600"
ERRORS=0

echo "Verifying signed images in ${DEPLOY_DIR}..."

# Verify U-Boot SPL
echo -n "  U-Boot SPL: "
if socsec verify --image "${DEPLOY_DIR}/u-boot-spl.bin" \
    --key "${PUBLIC_KEY}" --soc "${SOC}" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "PASS"
else
    echo "FAIL"
    ERRORS=$((ERRORS + 1))
fi

# Verify U-Boot proper
echo -n "  U-Boot:     "
if socsec verify --image "${DEPLOY_DIR}/u-boot.bin" \
    --key "${PUBLIC_KEY}" --soc "${SOC}" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "PASS"
else
    echo "FAIL"
    ERRORS=$((ERRORS + 1))
fi

# Verify FIT image (kernel)
echo -n "  FIT Image:  "
if [ -f "${DEPLOY_DIR}/fitImage" ]; then
    if fit_check_sign -f "${DEPLOY_DIR}/fitImage" \
        -k "${DEPLOY_DIR}/u-boot.dtb" 2>/dev/null; then
        echo "PASS"
    else
        echo "FAIL"
        ERRORS=$((ERRORS + 1))
    fi
else
    echo "SKIP (fitImage not found)"
fi

echo ""
if [ "${ERRORS}" -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "All signature verifications passed."
    exit 0
else
    echo "ERROR: ${ERRORS} verification(s) failed!"
    exit 1
fi
```

## Troubleshooting

    

### Issue: Board does not boot after OTP programming

    

**Symptom**: Board appears completely dead after programming OTP fuses. No serial output, no response.

**Cause**: The OTP security straps enable secure boot, but the flash contains unsigned images (or images signed with a different key).

**Solution**:

1. Close the security jumper to bypass secure boot
2. Power cycle the board
3. Flash correctly signed images via UART recovery or SPI programmer
4. Open the security jumper and power cycle again

### Issue: socsec reports “signature verification failed”

    

**Symptom**: `socsec verify` fails on a signed image that previously verified correctly.

**Cause**: The image was modified after signing (e.g., by a post-processing step in the build), or you are verifying with the wrong public key.

**Solution**:

1. Confirm you are using the correct public key that matches the signing private key
2. Check that no build steps modify the image after the signing step
3. Re-sign the image and verify immediately:
    
```
socsec sign --image u-boot-spl.bin --key private.pem \
    --algorithm RSA4096_SHA256 --soc 2600 --output signed.bin
socsec verify --image signed.bin --key public.pem --soc 2600
```

### Issue: FIT image signature verification fails in U-Boot

    

**Symptom**: U-Boot prints `Bad Data Hash` or `RSA signature verification failed` when booting the kernel.

**Cause**: The FIT image was signed with a key that does not match the public key embedded in U-Boot’s DTB, or the FIT image was modified after signing.

**Solution**:

1. Verify that the `UBOOT_SIGN_KEYNAME` in your build configuration matches the key filename (without extension)
2. Rebuild both U-Boot and the FIT image together (the public key is embedded in U-Boot’s DTB during FIT signing)
3. Ensure the `-r` flag is passed to `mkimage` to mark the key as required

### Issue: OTP programming fails with “protected region” error

    

**Symptom**: `socsec otp_prog` reports a write-protection error.

**Cause**: The OTP region you are attempting to write has already been programmed. OTP bits can only transition from 0 to 1, never from 1 to 0.

**Solution**:

1. Read the current OTP contents: `socsec otp_read --port /dev/ttyUSB0 --baud 115200 --output current_otp.bin`
2. Compare against your target configuration to identify conflicting bits
3. If the existing OTP data conflicts with your new key, you cannot change it. The board is permanently bound to the previously programmed key.

### Debug Commands

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Check OTP fuse contents from a running BMC (Linux)</span>
devmem 0x1e6f2000 32   <span class="c"># OTP configuration word 0</span>
devmem 0x1e6f2004 32   <span class="c"># OTP configuration word 1</span>

<span class="c"># Read security strap register</span>
devmem 0x1e6e2510 32   <span class="c"># SCU510 — hardware strap status</span>

<span class="c"># Check U-Boot verified boot status (from U-Boot shell)</span>
<span class="c"># At U-Boot prompt:</span>
<span class="nb">env </span>print verified_boot
iminfo <span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">loadaddr</span><span class="k">}</span>      <span class="c"># Show FIT image info including signature status</span>

<span class="c"># View kernel boot log for FIT verification</span>
dmesg | <span class="nb">grep</span> <span class="nt">-i</span> <span class="s2">"verified</span><span class="se">\|</span><span class="s2">signature</span><span class="se">\|</span><span class="s2">secure"</span>
```

</div></div>

## Overview

    

Multi-host support allows a single BMC to manage two or more host systems from one firmware image. This is common in high-density server platforms such as twin-server chassis, multi-node sleds, and blade enclosures where dedicating a BMC per host is impractical due to cost, power, or space constraints.

In a multi-host OpenBMC deployment, the BMC communicates with each host over dedicated IPMB (Intelligent Platform Management Bus) links — one I2C bus per host — and maintains independent state machines, sensor namespaces, and Redfish resource trees for each host. The systemd service manager uses template units to instantiate per-host services, while D-Bus object paths are indexed by host number to keep each host’s state isolated.

This guide walks you through the complete multi-host architecture: how IPMB bridges messages between the BMC and each host, how systemd template units and D-Bus object paths provide per-host isolation, how to configure your machine layer for N hosts, and how Redfish exposes each host as a separate ComputerSystem resource.

**Key concepts covered:**

* Single-BMC-to-N-host architecture over IPMB
* IPMB bridge daemon configuration (I2C bus assignment, address routing)
* Per-host state management with systemd template units
* D-Bus object path multiplexing (`/xyz/openbmc_project/state/host0`, `host1`, …)
* Redfish ComputerSystem mapping for each host
* Yocto/BitBake configuration for multi-host builds

Multi-host support requires careful hardware design. Each host needs a dedicated I2C bus for IPMB communication. Verify your baseboard schematic provides separate I2C controllers or mux channels for each host before implementing the software configuration.

Multi-host is distinct from multi-node MCTP/PLDM topologies. This guide covers two approaches: (1) IPMI-based multi-host where each host has a traditional IPMB link to the BMC, and (2) satellite processor (OpenBIC) multi-host where Bridge ICs act as local agents offloading the BMC. For PLDM-based multi-endpoint management, see the [MCTP & PLDM Guide](/openbmc-guide-tutorial/docs/05-advanced/01-mctp-pldm-guide.html).

---

## Architecture

    

### Multi-Host System Topology

    

A multi-host BMC manages N hosts through dedicated IPMB channels. Each host has its own I2C bus, power control GPIOs, and an independent state machine on the BMC side.

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  Multi-Host BMC Architecture                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│   │                     BMC (AST2600)                        │  │
│   │                                                          │  │
│   │  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐          │  │
│   │  │ State Mgr  │  │ State Mgr  │  │ State Mgr  │  ...     │  │
│   │  │  (host0)   │  │  (host1)   │  │  (host2)   │          │  │
│   │  └─────┬──────┘  └─────┬──────┘  └─────┬──────┘          │  │
│   │        │               │               │                 │  │
│   │  ┌─────┴───────────────┴───────────────┴──────────────┐  │  │
│   │  │              D-Bus (phosphor-dbus)                 │  │  │
│   │  │  /xyz/openbmc_project/state/host0                  │  │  │
│   │  │  /xyz/openbmc_project/state/host1                  │  │  │
│   │  │  /xyz/openbmc_project/state/host2                  │  │  │
│   │  └─────┬───────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────┘  │  │
│   │        │               │               │                 │  │
│   │  ┌─────┴──────┐  ┌─────┴───────┐  ┌────┴───────┐         │  │
│   │  │ IPMB Bridge│  │ IPMB Bridge │  │ IPMB Bridge│         │  │
│   │  │  (I2C-1)   │  │  (I2C-2)    │  │  (I2C-3)   │         │  │
│   │  └─────┬──────┘  └─────┬───────┘  └─────┬──────┘         │  │
│   └────────┼───────────────┼────────────────┼────────────────┘  │
│            │               │                │                   │
│      ┌─────┴──────┐  ┌─────┴──────┐  ┌──────┴─────┐             │
│      │   Host 0   │  │   Host 1   │  │   Host 2   │             │
│      │ (CPU/BIOS) │  │ (CPU/BIOS) │  │ (CPU/BIOS) │             │
│      └────────────┘  └────────────┘  └────────────┘             │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

</div></div>

### IPMB Communication Model

    

Each host communicates with the BMC over a dedicated I2C bus using the IPMB protocol. The BMC acts as the IPMB master (address 0x20) and each host baseboard management controller or satellite controller responds at a host-specific slave address.

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  IPMB Message Flow                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│   BMC (Master 0x20)                                             │
│    │                                                            │
│    ├── I2C Bus 1 ──── IPMB Channel 1 ──── Host 0 (Slave 0x70)   │
│    │                                                            │
│    ├── I2C Bus 2 ──── IPMB Channel 2 ──── Host 1 (Slave 0x72)   │
│    │                                                            │
│    ├── I2C Bus 3 ──── IPMB Channel 3 ──── Host 2 (Slave 0x74)   │
│    │                                                            │
│    └── I2C Bus 4 ──── IPMB Channel 4 ──── Host 3 (Slave 0x76)   │
│                                                                 │
│   IPMB Request Frame:                                           │
│   ┌────────┬────────┬──────┬──────┬────────┬─────────┬────────┐ │
│   │ rsSA   │ NetFn/ │ Chk1 │ rqSA │ rqSeq/ │ Command │ Data + │ │
│   │ (Slave)│ rsLUN  │      │(BMC) │ rqLUN  │         │  Chk2  │ │
│   └────────┴────────┴──────┴──────┴────────┴─────────┴────────┘ │
│                                                                 │
│   Key fields:                                                   │
│   ── rsSA:  Responder slave address (host-specific)             │
│   ── rqSA:  Requester slave address (BMC = 0x20)                │
│   ── NetFn: Network function (Chassis, Sensor, App, etc.)       │
│   ── Chk1/2: Header and data checksums                          │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

</div></div>

### D-Bus Object Path Convention

    

Multi-host OpenBMC uses a numeric suffix on D-Bus object paths to identify each host. All phosphor services that are host-aware follow this naming convention.

<div class="table-wrapper">
| D-Bus Object Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `/xyz/openbmc_project/state/host0` | Host 0 power/boot state |
| `/xyz/openbmc_project/state/host1` | Host 1 power/boot state |
| `/xyz/openbmc_project/state/chassis0` | Chassis 0 power state |
| `/xyz/openbmc_project/state/chassis1` | Chassis 1 power state |
| `/xyz/openbmc_project/control/host0/boot` | Host 0 boot settings |
| `/xyz/openbmc_project/control/host1/boot` | Host 1 boot settings |
| `/xyz/openbmc_project/sensors/temperature/host0_cpu_temp` | Host 0 CPU temperature |
| `/xyz/openbmc_project/sensors/temperature/host1_cpu_temp` | Host 1 CPU temperature |
| `/xyz/openbmc_project/inventory/system/host0` | Host 0 inventory |
| `/xyz/openbmc_project/inventory/system/host1` | Host 1 inventory |

</div>

### Redfish Resource Mapping

    

Each host maps to a separate Redfish ComputerSystem resource. The BMC itself is exposed as a single Manager that manages all hosts.

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  Redfish Resource Tree                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  /redfish/v1/                                                   │
│  ├── Managers/                                                  │
│  │   └── bmc                          ← Single BMC manager      │
│  │       ├── ManagerType: "BMC"                                 │
│  │       └── Links/ManagerForServers:                           │
│  │           ├── /redfish/v1/Systems/host0                      │
│  │           ├── /redfish/v1/Systems/host1                      │
│  │           └── /redfish/v1/Systems/host2                      │
│  │                                                              │
│  ├── Systems/                                                   │
│  │   ├── host0                        ← Host 0 ComputerSystem   │
│  │   │   ├── PowerState: "On"                                   │
│  │   │   ├── Actions/ComputerSystem.Reset                       │
│  │   │   ├── Processors/                                        │
│  │   │   ├── Memory/                                            │
│  │   │   └── LogServices/                                       │
│  │   ├── host1                        ← Host 1 ComputerSystem   │
│  │   │   ├── PowerState: "Off"                                  │
│  │   │   ├── ...                                                │
│  │   └── host2                        ← Host 2 ComputerSystem   │
│  │       ├── ...                                                │
│  │                                                              │
│  └── Chassis/                                                   │
│      ├── chassis0                     ← Physical chassis 0      │
│      │   ├── Thermal/                                           │
│      │   ├── Power/                                             │
│      │   └── Links/ComputerSystems:                             │
│      │       └── /redfish/v1/Systems/host0                      │
│      └── chassis1                     ← Physical chassis 1      │
│          └── ...                                                │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

</div></div>

### Key Dependencies

    

* **phosphor-state-manager**: Provides per-host state machines (host, chassis, BMC states)
* **ipmb-bridge / ipmbd**: Routes IPMI messages between the BMC and each host over I2C
* **phosphor-host-ipmid**: Handles IPMI commands, instantiated per host
* **bmcweb**: Serves Redfish with per-host ComputerSystem resources
* **phosphor-gpio-monitor**: Monitors per-host GPIO signals (power button, reset, etc.)

---

## Configuration

    

### Machine Configuration for Multi-Host

    

Define the number of hosts and IPMB bus assignments in your machine configuration.

```bitbake
# meta-mymachine/conf/machine/mymachine.conf

# Number of host instances (0-indexed: host0, host1, ..., hostN-1)
OBMC_HOST_INSTANCES = "0 1 2 3"

# Map each host to an I2C bus for IPMB communication
OBMC_HOST_IPMB_BUSSES = "1 2 3 4"

# IPMB slave addresses per host (7-bit format)
OBMC_HOST_IPMB_ADDRESSES = "0x70 0x72 0x74 0x76"

# Include multi-host support packages
OBMC_MACHINE_FEATURES += "obmc-host-state-mgmt obmc-chassis-state-mgmt"

# Enable per-host state manager instances
VIRTUAL-RUNTIME_obmc-host-state-manager = "phosphor-state-manager-host"
VIRTUAL-RUNTIME_obmc-chassis-state-manager = "phosphor-state-manager-chassis"
```

### IPMB Bridge Daemon Configuration

    

The IPMB bridge daemon (`ipmbd`) runs one instance per host, each bound to a specific I2C bus. Configuration is typically done through systemd template units.

#### ipmbd Service Template

    

<div class="language-ini highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># /lib/systemd/system/ipmbd@.service
</span><span class="nn">[Unit]</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="py">Description</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">IPMB Bridge Daemon for host %i</span>
<span class="py">After</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">sys-subsystem-i2c-devices-i2c</span><span class="se">\x</span><span class="s">2d%i.device</span>
<span class="py">BindsTo</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">sys-subsystem-i2c-devices-i2c</span><span class="se">\x</span><span class="s">2d%i.device</span>
<span class="w">
</span><span class="nn">[Service]</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="py">Type</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">simple</span>
<span class="py">ExecStart</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">/usr/bin/ipmbd %i 0x20</span>
<span class="py">Restart</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">on-failure</span>
<span class="py">RestartSec</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">5</span>
<span class="w">
</span><span class="nn">[Install]</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="py">WantedBy</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">multi-user.target</span>
```

</div></div>

#### Enable IPMB for Each Host

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Enable ipmbd for I2C buses 1-4 (corresponding to hosts 0-3)</span>
systemctl <span class="nb">enable </span>ipmbd@1.service
systemctl <span class="nb">enable </span>ipmbd@2.service
systemctl <span class="nb">enable </span>ipmbd@3.service
systemctl <span class="nb">enable </span>ipmbd@4.service
```

</div></div>

```
            </span><span class="nl">"name"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"IPMB_HOST0"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"bus"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">

        </span><span class="p">},</span><span class="w">

            </span><span class="nl">"type"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"ipmb"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"name"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"IPMB_HOST1"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"bus"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">2</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"slave_address"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"0x72"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"host_instance"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="p">},</span><span class="w">

            </span><span class="nl">"type"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"ipmb"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"name"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"IPMB_HOST2"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"bus"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">3</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"slave_address"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"0x74"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"host_instance"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">2</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="p">},</span><span class="w">

            </span><span class="nl">"type"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"ipmb"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"name"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"IPMB_HOST3"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"bus"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mi">4</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
            </span><span class="nl">"slave_address"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"0x76"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">

</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
```

### I2C Device Tree Configuration

    

Each IPMB bus requires an I2C controller in the device tree. On AST2600, assign dedicated I2C controllers for each host.

```dts
/* IPMB I2C buses for multi-host */
&i2c1 {
    status = "okay";
    /* IPMB to Host 0 */
    multi-master;
    ipmb@20 {
        compatible = "ipmb-dev";
        reg = <0x20>;
    };
};

&i2c2 {
    status = "okay";
    /* IPMB to Host 1 */
    multi-master;
    ipmb@20 {
        compatible = "ipmb-dev";
        reg = <0x20>;
    };
};

&i2c3 {
    status = "okay";
    /* IPMB to Host 2 */
    multi-master;
    ipmb@20 {
        compatible = "ipmb-dev";
        reg = <0x20>;
    };
};

&i2c4 {
    status = "okay";
    /* IPMB to Host 3 */
    multi-master;
    ipmb@20 {
        compatible = "ipmb-dev";
        reg = <0x20>;
    };
};
```

The `multi-master` property enables I2C multi-master mode, which is required for IPMB because both the BMC and the host can initiate transactions on the same bus.

### Per-Host State Manager Configuration

    

The phosphor-state-manager uses systemd template units to create independent state machines per host.

#### Host State Template

    

<div class="language-ini highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># /lib/systemd/system/phosphor-host-state-manager@.service
</span><span class="nn">[Unit]</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="py">Description</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">Phosphor Host State Manager for host %i</span>
<span class="py">Wants</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">mapper-wait@-xyz-openbmc_project-state-host%i.service</span>
<span class="py">After</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">mapper-wait@-xyz-openbmc_project-state-host%i.service</span>
<span class="w">
</span><span class="nn">[Service]</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="py">Type</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">dbus</span>
<span class="py">BusName</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">xyz.openbmc_project.State.Host%i</span>
<span class="py">ExecStart</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">/usr/bin/phosphor-host-state-manager --host %i</span>
<span class="py">Restart</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">on-failure</span>
<span class="w">
</span><span class="nn">[Install]</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="py">WantedBy</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">multi-user.target</span>
```

</div></div>

#### Chassis State Template

    

<div class="language-ini highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># /lib/systemd/system/phosphor-chassis-state-manager@.service
</span><span class="nn">[Unit]</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="py">Description</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">Phosphor Chassis State Manager for chassis %i</span>
<span class="w">
</span><span class="nn">[Service]</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="py">Type</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">dbus</span>
<span class="py">BusName</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">xyz.openbmc_project.State.Chassis%i</span>
<span class="py">ExecStart</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">/usr/bin/phosphor-chassis-state-manager --chassis %i</span>

</span><span class="nn">[Install]</span><span class="w">

```

</div></div>

#### Enable Per-Host Services

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Enable state managers for all hosts</span>
<span class="k">for </span>i <span class="k">in </span>0 1 2 3<span class="p">;</span> <span class="k">do
    </span>systemctl <span class="nb">enable </span>phosphor-host-state-manager@<span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">i</span><span class="k">}</span>.service
    systemctl <span class="nb">enable </span>phosphor-chassis-state-manager@<span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">i</span><span class="k">}</span>.service
<span class="k">done</span>
```

</div></div>

### Build-Time Options

    

<div class="table-wrapper">
| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OBMC_HOST_INSTANCES` | `"0"` | Space-separated list of host instance numbers |
| `OBMC_HOST_IPMB_BUSSES` | `"1"` | I2C bus numbers for IPMB, one per host |
| `OBMC_HOST_IPMB_ADDRESSES` | `"0x70"` | 7-bit I2C slave addresses for each host |
| `OBMC_CHASSIS_INSTANCES` | `"0"` | Chassis instance numbers (may differ from host count) |
| `OBMC_HOST_STATE_MANAGER_MULTI` | `"1"` | Set to number of hosts to enable multi-host state manager |

</div>

## Porting Guide

    

Follow these steps to enable multi-host support on your platform.

### Step 1: Prerequisites

    

Ensure you have:

* Dedicated I2C buses from the BMC to each host (one per host)
* Per-host GPIO signals for power control (power button, reset, etc.)
* A working single-host OpenBMC image for your platform
* Device tree source for your baseboard

### Step 2: Update Device Tree

    

Add I2C controller nodes for each IPMB bus and configure multi-master mode.

```dts
/* In your machine device tree overlay */
/* aspeed-bmc-mymachine.dts */

&i2c1 {
    status = "okay";
    multi-master;
    /* Host 0 IPMB */
};

&i2c2 {
    status = "okay";
    multi-master;
    /* Host 1 IPMB */
};

/* Add per-host power control GPIOs */
&gpio0 {
    host0-power-enable {
        gpio-hog;
        gpios = <ASPEED_GPIO(A, 0) GPIO_ACTIVE_HIGH>;
        output-low;
        line-name = "host0-power-enable";
    };

    host1-power-enable {
        gpio-hog;
        gpios = <ASPEED_GPIO(A, 1) GPIO_ACTIVE_HIGH>;
        output-low;
        line-name = "host1-power-enable";
    };
};
```

### Step 3: Configure Machine Layer

    

Update your machine configuration to declare host instances and IPMB mappings.

```bitbake
# meta-mymachine/conf/machine/mymachine.conf

OBMC_HOST_INSTANCES = "0 1"

# Map host instances to I2C buses
OBMC_HOST_IPMB_BUSSES = "1 2"
OBMC_HOST_IPMB_ADDRESSES = "0x70 0x72"

# Per-host power GPIO configuration
OBMC_POWER_GPIO_HOST0 = "host0-power-enable"
OBMC_POWER_GPIO_HOST1 = "host1-power-enable"
```

### Step 4: Create Systemd Target Dependencies

    

Define per-host boot targets so that services start in the correct order for each host.

<div class="language-ini highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># meta-mymachine/recipes-phosphor/state/files/host0-boot.target
</span><span class="nn">[Unit]</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="py">Description</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">Host 0 Boot Target</span>
<span class="py">Wants</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">ipmbd@1.service</span>
<span class="py">Wants</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">phosphor-host-state-manager@0.service</span>
<span class="py">Wants</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">phosphor-chassis-state-manager@0.service</span>
<span class="py">After</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">ipmbd@1.service</span>
```

</div></div>

<div class="language-ini highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># meta-mymachine/recipes-phosphor/state/files/host1-boot.target
</span><span class="nn">[Unit]</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="py">Description</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">Host 1 Boot Target</span>
<span class="py">Wants</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">ipmbd@2.service</span>
<span class="py">Wants</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">phosphor-host-state-manager@1.service</span>
<span class="py">Wants</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">phosphor-chassis-state-manager@1.service</span>
<span class="py">After</span><span class="p">=</span><span class="s">ipmbd@2.service</span>
```

</div></div>

### Step 5: Add IPMB Bridge Recipe Append

    

Create a bbappend to install per-host ipmbd service configurations.

```bitbake
# meta-mymachine/recipes-phosphor/ipmi/ipmb-bridge_%.bbappend

FILESEXTRAPATHS:prepend := "${THISDIR}/${PN}:"

SRC_URI += " \
    file://ipmb-channels.json \
"

do_install:append() {
    install -d ${D}${datadir}/ipmb-bridge
    install -m 0644 ${WORKDIR}/ipmb-channels.json \
        ${D}${datadir}/ipmb-bridge/
}
```

### Step 6: Build and Verify

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Build the multi-host image</span>
bitbake obmc-phosphor-image

<span class="c"># After flashing, verify all host state managers are running</span>
systemctl status phosphor-host-state-manager@0
systemctl status phosphor-host-state-manager@1

<span class="c"># Verify IPMB bridges</span>
systemctl status ipmbd@1
systemctl status ipmbd@2

<span class="c"># Check D-Bus objects</span>
busctl tree xyz.openbmc_project.State.Host0
busctl tree xyz.openbmc_project.State.Host1
```

</div></div>
---

## Code Examples

    

### Example 1: Querying Per-Host State via D-Bus

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Get power state for each host</span>
<span class="k">for </span>i <span class="k">in </span>0 1 2 3<span class="p">;</span> <span class="k">do
    </span><span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"Host </span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">i</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2"> state:"</span>
    busctl get-property xyz.openbmc_project.State.Host<span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">i</span><span class="k">}</span> <span class="se">\</span>
        /xyz/openbmc_project/state/host<span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">i</span><span class="k">}</span> <span class="se">\</span>
        xyz.openbmc_project.State.Host <span class="se">\</span>
        CurrentHostState
<span class="k">done</span>

<span class="c"># Example output:</span>
<span class="c"># Host 0 state: s "xyz.openbmc_project.State.Host.HostState.Running"</span>
<span class="c"># Host 1 state: s "xyz.openbmc_project.State.Host.HostState.Off"</span>
<span class="c"># Host 2 state: s "xyz.openbmc_project.State.Host.HostState.Running"</span>
<span class="c"># Host 3 state: s "xyz.openbmc_project.State.Host.HostState.Off"</span>
```

</div></div>

### Example 2: Power Control via Redfish

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c"># Power on Host 1</span>
curl <span class="nt">-k</span> <span class="nt">-u</span> root:0penBmc <span class="nt">-X</span> POST <span class="se">\</span>
    https://bmc-ip/redfish/v1/Systems/host1/Actions/ComputerSystem.Reset <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-H</span> <span class="s2">"Content-Type: application/json"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-d</span> <span class="s1">'{"ResetType": "On"}'</span>

<span class="c"># Graceful shutdown Host 0</span>
curl <span class="nt">-k</span> <span class="nt">-u</span> root:0penBmc <span class="nt">-X</span> POST <span class="se">\</span>
    https://bmc-ip/redfish/v1/Systems/host0/Actions/ComputerSystem.Reset <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-H</span> <span class="s2">"Content-Type: application/json"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
    <span class="nt">-d</span> <span class="s1">'{"ResetType": "GracefulShutdown"}'</span>

<span class="c"># Get all systems</span>
curl <span class="nt">-k</span> <span class="nt">-u</span> root:0penBmc <span class="se">\</span>
    https://bmc-ip/redfish/v1/Systems/

<span class="c"># Example response (abbreviated):</span>
<span class="c"># {</span>
<span class="c">#     "@odata.id": "/redfish/v1/Systems",</span>
<span class="c">#     "Members": [</span>
<span class="c">#         {"@odata.id": "/redfish/v1/Systems/host0"},</span>
<span class="c">#         {"@odata.id": "/redfish/v1/Systems/host1"},</span>
<span class="c">#         {"@odata.id": "/redfish/v1/Systems/host2"},</span>
<span class="c">#         {"@odata.id": "/redfish/v1/Systems/host3"}</span>
<span class="c">#     ],</span>
<span class="c">#     "Members@odata.count": 4</span>
<span class="c"># }</span>
```

### Example 3: Per-Host IPMB Communication

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">

```
<span class="c"># Send an IPMI Get Device ID command to Host 0 via IPMB channel 1</span>
ipmitool <span class="nt">-I</span> ipmb <span class="nt">-H</span> localhost <span class="nt">-t</span> 0x70 <span class="nt">-b</span> 1 raw 0x06 0x01

<span class="c"># Send the same command to Host 1 via IPMB channel 2</span>
ipmitool <span class="nt">-I</span> ipmb <span class="nt">-H</span> localhost <span class="nt">-t</span> 0x72 <span class="nt">-b</span> 2 raw 0x06 0x01

<span class="c"># Get chassis status for Host 0</span>
ipmitool <span class="nt">-I</span> ipmb <span class="nt">-H</span> localhost <span class="nt">-t</span> 0x70 <span class="nt">-b</span> 1 chassis status

<span class="c"># Get sensor list from Host 1</span>
ipmitool <span class="nt">-I</span> ipmb <span class="nt">-H</span> localhost <span class="nt">-t</span> 0x72 <span class="nt">-b</span> 2 sdr list
```

### Example 4: Host State Monitor Script

    

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight">
```
<span class="c">#!/bin/bash</span>
<span class="c"># monitor-hosts.sh - Monitor power state of all hosts</span>
<span class="c"># See: docs/examples/multi-host/</span>

<span class="nv">HOSTS</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s2">"0 1 2 3"</span>
<span class="nv">INTERVAL</span><span class="o">=</span>5

<span class="k">while </span><span class="nb">true</span><span class="p">;</span> <span class="k">do
    </span>clear
    <span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"=== Multi-Host Status (</span><span class="si">$(</span><span class="nb">date</span><span class="si">)</span><span class="s2">) ==="</span>
    <span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">""</span>
    <span class="k">for </span>h <span class="k">in</span> <span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">HOSTS</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="p">;</span> <span class="k">do
        </span><span class="nv">STATE</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="si">$(</span>busctl get-property <span class="se">\</span>
            xyz.openbmc_project.State.Host<span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">h</span><span class="k">}</span> <span class="se">\</span>
            /xyz/openbmc_project/state/host<span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">h</span><span class="k">}</span> <span class="se">\</span>
            xyz.openbmc_project.State.Host <span class="se">\</span>
            CurrentHostState 2>/dev/null | <span class="nb">awk</span> <span class="s1">'{print $2}'</span> | <span class="nb">tr</span> <span class="nt">-d</span> <span class="s1">'"'</span><span class="si">)</span>

        <span class="nv">CHASSIS</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="si">$(</span>busctl get-property <span class="se">\</span>
            xyz.openbmc_project.State.Chassis<span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">h</span><span class="k">}</span> <span class="se">\</span>
            /xyz/openbmc_project/state/chassis<span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">h</span><span class="k">}</span> <span class="se">\</span>
            xyz.openbmc_project.State.Chassis <span class="se">\</span>
            CurrentPowerState 2>/dev/null | <span class="nb">awk</span> <span class="s1">'{print $2}'</span> | <span class="nb">tr</span> <span class="nt">-d</span> <span class="s1">'"'</span><span class="si">)</span>

        <span class="c"># Extract short state name</span>
        <span class="nv">HOST_SHORT</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">STATE</span><span class="p">##*.</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">"</span>
        <span class="nv">CHASSIS_SHORT</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">CHASSIS</span><span class="p">##*.</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">"</span>

        <span class="nb">printf</span> <span class="s2">"  Host %-2d : %-12s  Chassis: %-12s</span><span class="se">\n</span><span class="s2">"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
            <span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">h</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">"</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">HOST_SHORT</span><span class="k">:-</span><span class="nv">Unknown</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">"</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">CHASSIS_SHORT</span><span class="k">:-</span><span class="nv">Unknown</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">"</span>
    <span class="k">done
    </span><span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">""</span>
    <span class="nb">echo</span> <span class="s2">"Refreshing every </span><span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">INTERVAL</span><span class="k">}</span><span class="s2">s. Press Ctrl+C to stop."</span>
    <span class="nb">sleep</span> <span class="k">${</span><span class="nv">INTERVAL</span><span class="k">}</span>
<span class="k">done</span>
```

</div></div>
